title: Rubric-based behavioral evaluation framework wired into the loop as an advisory gate
description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 7. basicly has deterministic gates + advisory semantic review but no use-case-tied yes/no behavioral rubrics. Add catalog-authored rubric sources evaluated deterministic-where-possible else agent-judged, reported as an advisory gate promotable per work-type. See design proposal in docs/foundry-spike.md dimension 7.

## Acceptance Criteria

- New catalog source .basicly/core/rubrics/*.rubric.yaml (id, description, applies_to work-types, checks[] each kind deterministic|judged), authored as YAML and loaded/validated/linted like other catalog sources; sample rubrics ship
- basicly rubric eval <issue> selects the rubric by the bead work-type, runs deterministic checks via the verify runner (exit code answers yes/no) and dispatches judged checks via a review-style prompt through the agent-agnostic runner (handoff when no CLI), producing structured yes/no plus evidence verdicts
- The command emits a rubric gate via br gate report, non-required (advisory) by default and promotable via [policy] required_gates
- Tests cover source load/lint, work-type selection, deterministic eval with real exit codes, judged eval with a mocked/handoff runner, and gate emission; judged verdicts stay advisory (live-agent answer unverified, same bar as catalog review)
- pytest, ruff, pyright, and the projection gates stay green

title: Verify hook stages beyond pre-commit and rule on the config filename
description:
Investigate whether the shipped hooks really cover more than the pre-commit stage (expected: pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push — and whether post-commit/post-push are wanted). Verify against hooks.yaml and the installed git hooks. Then rule on the user's suggestion to genericize the .pre-commit-config.yaml filename (e.g. .hook-config.yaml) — note the filename is mandated by the pre-commit framework itself, so document the finding instead if a rename is impossible.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A verified list of which git stages the catalog ships hooks for, from hooks.yaml and pre-commit install stages
- An explicit answer on renaming .pre-commit-config.yaml, with rationale
- Docs updated where the pre-commit-only impression is created
close_reason: three git stages plus a claude agent hook verified; rename rejected (framework-mandated filename), readme clarified

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Verified: hooks.yaml ships pre-commit (identity-guard, pre-commit-script, catalog-lint), commit-msg (commit-msg-script, beads-commit-msg-script), pre-push (pre-push-script), and a Claude PreToolUse agent hook (protect-generated); all three git stages are installed in .git/hooks and every config entry carries an explicit stages: list. Ruling on the rename: .pre-commit-config.yaml is the pre-commit FRAMEWORK's mandated discovery filename — the tool manages every git stage despite its name, and a rename to .hook-config.yaml would break the tool and its editor/CI integrations. No rename; the README wiring line now spells this out. post-commit is supported by the framework but cannot block (the commit already exists), and git has no client-side post-push hook at all — so no after-commit/after-push hooks are warranted.

title: Identity: stamp the dispatched agent (and model) as attribution on landed commits and gate results
description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 1. Commits and gates carry only the human git identity; the runner name/model is known at dispatch and discarded (includeCoAuthoredBy is false). The D3 run-record (.basicly/usage/run-records.json) already holds agent+model per bead; this bead surfaces that provenance as attribution on the landed commit and the gate result.

## Acceptance Criteria

- run_record gains a latest_record(repo_root, bead_id) -> RunRecord | None accessor returning the most recent record for the bead (None when absent or empty).
- The landing merge commit carries agent attribution as git trailers sourced from the latest run-record: Harness-Runner: <agent>, plus Harness-Model: <model> when the run pinned one. No record -> the merge message is unchanged. The conventional subject and the trailing bead id are preserved so the commit-msg and beads hooks still pass.
- The verify gate records the runner: br gate report gets --actor <agent> and the model folded into the note, sourced from the latest run-record, for both the loop landing (loop._record_verify) and basicly verify --issue. No record -> no actor and the note is unchanged.
- Graceful when no run-record exists (verify run outside a dispatch): nothing breaks, no attribution added.
- Regression tests: the latest_record accessor; the merge message with and without a record; report_gate passing actor/model; the loop wiring reads the record.
- Architecture section 12.8 (and the dimension-1 attribution note) updated.
- pytest, ruff, and the projection checks stay green.

## Scope

Attribution from the existing run-record only: a merge-commit trailer and a gate actor. No per-agent bot identity (basicly-smzg), no commit signing or tamper-evidence, no new attribution source. Trailer chosen over a synthetic Co-Authored-By (no fake identity/email) per the and/or in the spike recommendation.

title: Stall watchdog tests asserted timing after a fixed sleep and went red on macos CI
description:
## Context

The three StallWatchdog tests shipped with basicly-kjc5.25 asserted a timing outcome after a fixed time.sleep, so whether they passed depended on how fast the host scheduled a background thread. They passed on ubuntu and windows and failed on macos-latest in run 30168113819, turning main red immediately after the kjc5.25 landing.

Could not be reproduced locally even under twelve CPU spinners, which is the point: a tuned sleep constant cannot be validated on the host that is not failing.

Fixed by waiting for the condition instead of for a duration (a _wait_until helper with a generous timeout), so the assertions no longer encode an assumption about host speed. Also corrected StallWatchdog._watch to measure idle time against a monotonic clock rather than accumulating the nominal poll interval - genuine correctness (a slow probe or an overrunning Event.wait made the flag arrive later than stall_after) though not the cause of the red.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the stall watchdog tests when they run on any supported runner then they assert the flag fired without depending on how fast the host schedules a thread, and main is green on all runners
close_reason: Fixed in 76f330b: condition-based waits plus monotonic idle measurement

title: Keep the copilot deny style when a config entry overrides the builtin
description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while exercising basicly-kjc5.59 through `basicly runner dry-run`. Not caused by
that change - reproduced on base `main` with a config that names no tier at all.

`[[runner.agents]]` replaces a builtin wholesale by design, so an entry overriding `copilot`
that does not restate `deny_style` gets `deny_style = None`. But `_inject_copilot_deny_tools`
still injects the permissions.yaml deny list onto that spec, and `format_command` then raises
because `deny_tools` is set with no style to spell it. The result is that **every** dispatch of
the overridden agent fails, including `basicly runner dry-run`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a scratch repo, write `basicly.toml` containing only:
   `[runner]` / `default = "copilot"` / `[[runner.agents]]` / `name = "copilot"` /
   `command = ["copilot", "-p", "{prompt}"]`
2. Run `basicly runner dry-run --runner copilot --prompt go`
3. Observed: `Error: runner 'copilot' sets deny_tools but has deny_style None; known: [...]`
   Expected: either the deny list is emitted in copilot's wire form, or it is not injected onto
   a spec that cannot express it.

The wholesale-replacement stance is deliberate and documented, so the fix is most likely to make
the injection carry the style it needs (or skip injecting when the spec cannot express it) rather
than to re-default the whole spec.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a config entry overriding the copilot agent without restating deny_style when any
  dispatch of it is formatted then the deny list is either emitted in copilot's wire form or not
  injected at all rather than raising, with a regression test covering the override path
acceptance_criteria: Given a config entry overriding the copilot agent without restating deny_style when any dispatch of it is formatted then the deny list is either emitted in copilots wire form or not injected at all rather than raising with a regression test covering the override path

title: Design: land after ship approval and fold the bead close into the merge commit
description:
Follow-up design track from basicly-flp. Today the loop lands a worktree at the build->verify transition, BEFORE the verify phase gate and the human ship checkpoint, and closes the bead in a separate post-ship tracker-only commit; merge_worktree also verifies twice (in the worktree post-rebase, then again on base via _record_verify, an identical tree). Proposed redesign: reorder to build -> verify (gate recorded from the worktree run) -> ship checkpoint -> land+close in one step, where the merge uses git merge --no-ff --no-commit, then closes the bead, flushes, stages .beads/issues.jsonl, and commits - one tracker-carrying merge commit per track, nothing lands on main before gates and human approval, and the duplicate base re-verify disappears. Must be designed against: feature fan-in (children land through the queue when all closed - their self-landing order changes), rework semantics after a landing failure, multi-track concurrency (base working-tree jsonl carrying another track's uncommitted claim at merge time), and loop_state phase derivation (verified currently implies a bound worktree + green gates; landing evidence moves). See the investigation and decision comments on basicly-flp.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A design comment (or architecture.md section update) covers phase reorder, fan-in, rework, concurrency, and phase-derivation impacts with a go/no-go recommendation; if go, implementation is decomposed into child beads. Full gate suite passes for anything landed.
close_reason: wontfix: NO-GO on the land-after-ship redesign. CI-cost driver already solved by flp; c9e5 and 4psl removed loop friction; residual governance+efficiency gains do not justify a high-risk reorder of phase-derivation/fan-in/rework/concurrency on a just-stabilized loop (P3). Full go/no-go analysis recorded in the design comment.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Scoped down by basicly-c9e5 (br redirect worktrees + engine-owned tracker commits): once c9e5 ships, the residual value here is governance only - landing before ship approval, and folding the close into the merge commit saves one CI-free engine commit. Re-evaluate go/no-go after c9e5.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text:
DESIGN GO/NO-GO: NO-GO (wontfix). Analysis of the proposed reorder (build -> verify[gate from worktree run] -> ship checkpoint -> land+close in one --no-ff --no-commit merge commit) against the required impact areas:

- Driver reassessment: the original motivation (pointless CI builds from tracker commits) was already solved by flp via paths-ignore .beads/** on the workflows + consumer template. c9e5 then made worktrees share the tracker via br redirect (no diverging issues.jsonl copy), and 4psl made the landing rebase conflict-free when work is committed. The loop is now stable and frictionless, so only two residual benefits remain: (1) governance - today code lands on main at build->verify, BEFORE the human ship checkpoint, so ship approval gates only teardown/close, not the merge; (2) efficiency - one fewer commit (fold close into the merge) and dropping the duplicate verify (worktree pre-merge check + base post-merge recorded run on an identical tree).

- Phase reorder impact: moving the merge to after the ship checkpoint inverts the state machine. loop_state currently derives 'verified' from a bound worktree + green required gate + a landed branch; landing evidence would move, so phase derivation and the _worktree_landed backstop (ship refuses an unlanded branch) both need reworking.
- Feature fan-in impact: children currently land through the serial merge queue at the parent build phase, and a child driven through its own loop self-lands at ITS ship. Landing the parent after ship changes when children land relative to parent approval - fan-in ordering and the 'already self-landed' accounting must be redesigned.
- Rework impact: a landing that fails AFTER a human has approved ship is a new failure mode (today landing precedes approval, so a landing failure reworks before any human gate). Recovery semantics post-approval are undefined.
- Concurrency impact: the --no-commit merge + stage .beads/issues.jsonl + commit would sweep any other in-flight track's uncommitted tracker claim sitting in the base working tree at merge time - a cross-track contamination risk the current commit_tracker_state path avoids.

- Decision: NO-GO. The CI-cost driver is solved; c9e5+4psl removed the friction; the residual wins are modest governance + efficiency on a P3, against a high-risk reorder spanning phase-derivation, fan-in, rework, and concurrency, on a loop that was just stabilized. Rejected alternative kept as-is. The one reason to revisit: if 'nothing lands on main before human ship approval' becomes a hard governance requirement (e.g. a production-agent/Foundry principle), reopen and decompose - but note deterministic verify gates already pass before landing, so the ship checkpoint is effectively a final formality today.

title: release uploads a stray gitignore asset from the build output dir
description:
The release workflow runs `uv build` then uploads `files: dist/*` (.github/workflows/release.yml:156). `uv build` writes a 1-byte `dist/.gitignore` (contents `*`) into the output dir, and the wildcard glob sweeps it onto the GitHub release page as a stray attachment alongside the real wheel and sdist.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Tag a release (push a `v*` tag) so the release job runs.
2. Open the published release and look at the Assets list.
3. A 1-byte `.gitignore` appears as an asset next to `basicly-<v>-py3-none-any.whl` and `basicly-<v>.tar.gz`.

Reproduced locally: `uv build --out-dir <dir>` emits a `.gitignore` (1 byte, contents `*`) beside the wheel and tarball.

## Root Cause
`files: dist/*` matches every file uv drops in `dist/`, including its scratch `.gitignore`, so the glob is too broad.
acceptance_criteria: release.yml uploads only dist/*.whl and dist/*.tar.gz; the stray dist/.gitignore no longer appears as a release asset; a check asserts the upload glob does not use a bare dist/* wildcard

title: single-source scoped rules: stop emitting .github/instructions by default
description:
VS Code loads both .claude/rules/*.md and .github/instructions/*.instructions.md with no dedup — it name-dedupes only skills (user-shared findings from a separate research session, 2026-07-16; metadata-alignment hypotheses were tested and disproved there). Path-scoped guidance therefore double-loads in VS Code for every consumer. That session adopted single-source emission (scoped rules to .claude/rules only, .github/instructions twins swept, a verifier failing if they reappear) — a basicly install refresh in a repo with that policy would regress it, so this must land before the next consumer refresh.

Change the default projection so scoped rules emit to .claude/rules/ only:
- copilot target keeps .github/copilot-instructions.md (root trio unchanged — each file has a distinct native reader)
- skills stay dual-emitted (.claude/skills + .agents/skills): Claude reads only the former, Codex only the latter, and VS Code safely name-dedupes them
- install/uninstall sweep previously manifest-tracked .github/instructions/*.instructions.md files in consumers
- trade-off, accepted: github.com-side Copilot (PR code review, cloud agent) loses path-scoped rules and keeps only the root copilot-instructions.md

## Acceptance Criteria
- basicly build/install no longer emits .github/instructions/*.instructions.md; basicly's own two files (python-style, test-discipline) are swept from .github/instructions/
- .github/copilot-instructions.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and .claude/rules/*.md output is unchanged
- skills remain dual-emitted to .claude/skills and .agents/skills
- a consumer re-running basicly install has its stale .github/instructions projections removed (manifest-driven)
- docs/architecture.md targets section records the single-source policy and the github.com trade-off
- tests cover the removed target and the stale-file sweep

title: Copilot usage extraction: credits from session usage checkpoint
description:
## Context

Reopened and re-prioritised 2026-07-29 after probing the live copilot CLI. The premise
recorded in `src/basicly/runner.py:153` is wrong and must be corrected with this work:
copilot does report token usage. The comment says its result event "carries premium-request
counts, not tokens", which is true of that one event and false as a generalisation.

Verified against `copilot -p ... --output-format json` plus the persisted session store:

- `result.usage` carries only `premiumRequests`, `totalApiDurationMs`, `sessionDurationMs`
  and `codeChanges` - no tokens. This is what the earlier probe saw.
- `session.usage_checkpoint.data` carries `totalNanoAiu` and `totalPremiumRequests`.
- `assistant.message.data` carries `model` and `outputTokens`.
- `model.call_start.data` carries `model` per call.
- `session.shutdown.data.modelMetrics.<modelId>` carries the whole thing, keyed by model:
  `requests{count,cost}`, `usage{inputTokens,outputTokens,cacheReadTokens,cacheWriteTokens,
  reasoningTokens}`, `totalNanoAiu`, and `tokenDetails`.

Observed on a one-word probe: inputTokens 24210, cacheWriteTokens 24208, outputTokens 4,
totalNanoAiu 6056400000 - that is 6.0564 AI credits.

The extraction wrinkle: `session.shutdown` is **not** emitted on stdout in headless `-p`
mode. It is persisted to the session store. So the reader is two-step - take
`result.sessionId` from the stream, then read that session's `events.jsonl`. The store path
is machine-local and must never be committed; it needs a config-overridable base rather than
a hardcoded home-relative path.

Because `modelMetrics` is already keyed by model id, this is the richest calibration carrier
of any adapter we have - it supplies the per-model token counts and a native cost figure that
basicly-jr0l.21 needs, for a family where nothing is recorded today.

Scope: `src/basicly/runner.py`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a completed copilot dispatch when its usage is read then the run record carries the
  per-model input output cache-read and cache-write token counts and the AI-credit cost taken
  from the session shutdown model metrics rather than the chars-over-four transcript estimate,
  and given a dispatch whose session store is absent or unreadable then the estimate fallback
  is used and recorded as an estimate rather than reported as measured, with tests
design: Do not discover the state path - dictate it. RunnerSpec gains a state_env naming the variable that relocates the family's state root: COPILOT_HOME for copilot and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for claude, both verified present in the shipped binaries; unset for codex, which is not installed here and must not be guessed. run() already injects dispatch env (BR_MODEL at runner.py:568, GIT_AUTHOR and GIT_COMMITTER for the bot identity), so set state_env to a harness-owned directory under the gitignored .basicly/usage tree and read usage from a location known by construction. Verified 2026-07-29: with COPILOT_HOME pointed at a scratch dir the session landed in that dir's session-state and not in the real home, and the dispatch still exited 0 because copilot auth comes from the gh credential store rather than from COPILOT_HOME. This removes the platform path table entirely - no home-directory guessing across Windows, Linux, macOS and WSL, and no wslpath mapping for a Windows binary invoked from WSL - and it makes the path derive from the repo root so nothing machine-specific can reach a committed file. Side benefit: per-dispatch state dirs make concurrent lanes hermetic, which they are not today. Residual risks to handle in the work: a Windows binary reached from WSL needs a Windows-shaped value, which is the one real platform branch and belongs in table-driven test data rather than host-dependent logic per the platform-hermetic rule; a consumer whose auth does live in the copilot home breaks on relocation, so an empty state dir after a failed dispatch must fall back to the default home and record that it did; and a family with no known state_env falls through to usage-unmeasurable, which basicly-jr0l.35 governs.
acceptance_criteria: Given a completed copilot dispatch when its usage is read then the run record carries the per-model input output cache-read and cache-write token counts and the AI-credit cost taken from the session shutdown model metrics rather than the chars-over-four transcript estimate, and given a dispatch whose session store is absent or unreadable then the estimate fallback is used and recorded as an estimate rather than reported as measured, with tests

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: User-supplied rate 2026-07-22 (unverified, AFAIK-grade): 1 copilot credit = 0.01 USD. That resolves the unit question: convert totalNanoAiu to USD as nanoAiu / 1e9 * 0.01 and keep RunRecord.cost USD-denominated - no unit-aware field needed. Verify the rate against GitHub billing docs (or 'copilot billing') before hardcoding; the probe example totalNanoAiu=6044400000 would be 6.0444 credits = 0.060444 USD.

title: Guardrails: runner output secret-redaction plus egress-policy seam
description:
From spike basicly-zv48 dimension 2. Captured runner stdout/stderr is never inspected/filtered/egress-limited. Redact secrets from persisted/surfaced runner output and optionally assert a network-restricted sandbox for headless runs.

Investigation (2026-07-18): run_record.py already never persists output (only a redacted command), so the gap is the surfaced/live RunResult.stdout/stderr, emitted raw by the CLI runner run and read by the loop/rubrics. The yzyd secret-scan hook (.basicly/core/hooks/secret-scan.py) has a high-signal pattern set to reuse, but it is a standalone stdlib hook (not importable), so a sibling redact module in src/basicly mirrors its patterns. Egress: basicly cannot portably network-sandbox a generic subprocess; that is agent-layer (codex sandbox = basicly-t0kt, claude/copilot config), so this task documents the egress posture rather than building a speculative seam (user-scoped 2026-07-18).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A new redact module redacts high-signal secret patterns (private-key header, aws/github/slack/google/openai tokens, slack webhook, and the generic secret-named assignment with placeholder filtering) from arbitrary text, replacing each hit with a labeled placeholder; secret-free text is returned unchanged.
- runner.run applies redaction to captured stdout and stderr so every surfaced/persisted RunResult carries redacted output (guardrail at the source); dry-run and handoff results (empty output) are unaffected.
- The redaction patterns mirror the secret-scan hook (basicly-yzyd) as the sibling detector, noted in a comment so the two stay in step.
- Egress is documented as delegated to the agent-layer sandbox (codex basicly-t0kt, claude/copilot config); basicly redacts output but does not sandbox a generic subprocess. No speculative seam is added.
- Deterministic tests cover each secret pattern class, secret-free passthrough, and run() redacting both stdout and stderr.

title: Research spike: lefthook vs pre-commit as the basicly hook runner
description:
Open question surfaced by basicly-x5gh: pre-commit as the hook runner forces every consumer to have pre-commit provisioned (uvx works, but it is a Python tool with an activation seam that just bit us on a fresh repo). Evaluate whether lefthook is objectively a better fit for basicly's hook distribution, or whether pre-commit stays.

Produce a decision doc that objectively lists the positives and negatives of each across the dimensions that actually matter for basicly, then recommends one:

- Consumer runtime cost: lefthook is a single static binary (no Python/runtime dep); pre-commit needs Python + provisioning (uv/uvx). basicly consumers reliably have uv, not necessarily pip/pre-commit.
- Cross-platform including Windows and WSL (a hard basicly constraint).
- Hook stage coverage basicly relies on: pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push.
- Config format and projection fit: how cleanly each maps to basicly's catalog -> generated wiring (.pre-commit-config.yaml today) and the managed-block rewrite (ruamel round-trip, basicly-wd7u).
- Speed and parallelism of hook execution.
- Ecosystem, maturity, maintenance, and migration cost off pre-commit.
- Whether either removes the auto-activation footgun entirely (e.g. lefthook install vs pre-commit install).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A written comparison (docs or tracker comment) enumerating pros and cons of lefthook vs pre-commit against the dimensions above, ending in a clear objective recommendation with rationale and a migration-cost estimate if it recommends switching. Decide scope of any follow-up implementation beads when picked up.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Decision: KEEP pre-commit (see docs/hook-runner-decision.md). Decisive factor: every projected hook runs 'uv run python', so Python/uv are required regardless of runner - lefthook's static-binary advantage is nullified, and it would add a Go-binary acquisition seam with no uv-native path while not removing activation (already fixed in basicly-x5gh). No implementation follow-up bead: recommendation is status quo. Reconsider triggers recorded in the doc (consumers lose uv; checks go Python-free; measured speed complaint; provisioning seam regresses). The runner-agnostic seam in hooks.yaml is kept so reopening stays cheap.

title: Loop landing conflicts on tracker state when base .beads is dirty at land time
description: Discovered 2026-07-20 landing basicly-5wpn through the harness loop. At the build->verify landing advance, the engine committed accumulated base .beads dirt directly to base main (a chore(beads) sync commit), then rebased the harness branch onto the new base. The harness branch carries its own tracked .beads/issues.jsonl snapshot (from the provisioning claim commit) of the SAME bead the base commit just rewrote, so the rebase hits a one-line conflict on that issue in issues.jsonl. It recurs every rework attempt (each landing re-flushes the mutated DB, producing a new divergent line) and escalated at the rework cap, leaving TWO redundant chore(beads) commits on main plus a dirty base tree and the code stranded uncommitted in the worktree. Matches the beads-tracker-vs-loop-worktrees hazard (never commit issues.jsonl on a harness branch). Repro: claim+classify a leaf task, let provisioning leave base .beads dirty, run loop advance to land. Fix direction: before rebasing the harness branch, reset/checkout the branch's .beads/issues.jsonl to base (or exclude it from the branch entirely so only the redirect-shared DB carries tracker state), and ensure base .beads is committed cleanly before the rebase rather than mid-landing. Recovered 5wpn via the sanctioned base-checkout path.
close_reason: fixed the loop landing: added a worktree-readiness precondition so an uncommitted or empty branch blocks with clear guidance instead of a misreported rebase conflict that burned rework and escalated; not-ready no longer spends a rework attempt; documented commit-before-advance in the harness-loop skill; regression tests added; verified against real git

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Root-cause correction (my original description was wrong). Reproduced with real git: the failure was NOT an issues.jsonl merge conflict. The agent's work was never committed on the harness branch, so merge_worktree's git rebase aborted with 'cannot rebase: you have unstaged changes' — a non-zero exit that line 185 misclassified as 'rebase-conflicts'. With the work committed, rebasing onto a tracker-advanced base succeeds cleanly (the code commit does not touch .beads, and base already carries the advanced tracker line). Confirmed CASE A (dirty->abort) vs CASE B (committed->clean rebase). Two real defects fixed: (1) no worktree-readiness precondition before rebasing; (2) an operator-fixable state burned rework and escalated with a misleading message. Fix: _worktree_land_readiness bails before touching base with a clear 'commit the work on <branch>' message when the tree is dirty or the branch has no commits ahead; _verify_and_land and merge_queue treat 'not-ready' as a plain block, not a rework attempt. Verified against real git for dirty/committed/empty/untracked-only cases; new regression tests in test_merge.py; harness-loop skill now tells the operator to commit on the branch before advancing.

title: Skill evals: prove distributed skills actually change agent behavior
description:
We distribute a catalog of skills (core + technology-scoped) but have NO evidence any of them actually do their job: whether a skill reliably TRIGGERS on the situations its description claims, and whether loading it measurably IMPROVES the agent's output vs not having it. Without evals we cannot tell a working skill from dead weight, catch a regression when a skill is edited, or justify what ships in the always-on baseline.

Goal: add an eval harness plus per-skill eval cases that measure (a) trigger accuracy (does the skill fire when it should and stay quiet when it should not) and (b) behavioral lift (does the guidance change the outcome on representative tasks). Reference approach to adapt: https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/tree/main/evals (eval cases per skill run against a model).

Scope to decide when picked up: eval file format and where cases live in the catalog; a basicly command to run them (and optionally a CI gate); which skills get cases first (start with the core universal skills and the highest-value tech skills); how to score trigger vs lift; cost/model controls so the suite is affordable to run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An eval harness exists and is documented; at least the core universal skills have eval cases covering trigger accuracy and behavioral lift.
- Running the evals produces a pass/fail (or scored) report a human can act on; a deliberately broken/removed skill is caught.
- The format and how to add a case per skill are documented (catalog-authoring or a dedicated doc). Full gate suite passes.
acceptance_criteria: Given the skill eval harness when it runs then it reports per-skill trigger accuracy and behavioral lift as an actionable pass-fail report a deliberately removed skill is caught and the case format plus how to add one per skill is documented with the full gate suite green

title: An answered retry escalation cannot be acted on because nothing clears the rework counter
description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1` hit the merge rework cap, so the supervisor escalated it to the decision
queue asking "retry, re-dispatch, or park?". The operator answered `retry` with evidence that the
gate failure was not the lane's work. **The answer cannot be carried out.**

`policy.record_rework` only ever increments and `policy.rework_attempts` only reads; there is no
clear, reset, or decrement anywhere, and `basicly policy rework` exposes only `--record`. So the
counter stays at the cap, and the next landing attempt escalates again immediately. The queue item
is answered but the lane cannot move.

The operator's only levers are both wrong: raise `[policy] max_rework` in config, which loosens
the cap for *every* node in the repo, or land the lane by hand, which is exactly what
basicly-kjc5.22's acceptance criterion forbids. The escalation therefore offers three choices and
implements none of them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Let a lane fail its landing gate until `rework: N/N attempts - ESCALATE (cap reached)`.
2. `basicly loop answer <decision-id> "retry"` — succeeds.
3. `basicly loop advance <lane>` — blocks and re-escalates at once; `basicly policy rework <lane> --gate merge` still reports the cap.
4. Expected: an answered `retry` lets exactly one further attempt through, without changing the repo-wide cap.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
acceptance_criteria: Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests

title: A flaky gate consumes a lane's rework budget as if the work were wrong
description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1`'s landing failed its `verify full` gate on
`tests/test_integration_loop.py::test_landing_blocks_instead_of_reworking_an_uncommitted_worktree`,
which failed with the known `br` clock defect (`updated_at: cannot be before created_at`). The
lane's own commit was three documentation files under `.basicly/core/skills/python/` and its two
projections — it cannot affect that test. Re-running the test in the lane's own worktree
immediately afterwards: 1 fail, 2 passes, no change in between.

The harness charged the lane a rework attempt for it, reached the cap, and escalated it to a human.
So a pre-existing upstream flake is scored exactly like a merit failure, and it cost the run its
acceptance criterion — two of three lanes landed unattended, the third was escalated for something
it did not do.

This is the harness-side half of the tracker defect that `basicly-vkh0` exists to remove; filing it
separately because the fix is different. `vkh0` stops the flake existing. This bead is about the
engine having no way to tell "the gate is unreliable" from "the work is wrong", so a flake silently
consumes a lane's bounded rework budget.

Design note: `basicly-kjc5.52` (fingerprint the environment behind a gate result) is adjacent — a
gate result that carries provenance is what would let a re-run be compared rather than merely
repeated.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Land a lane whose verify suite contains a test that fails intermittently for reasons unrelated to the lane's diff.
2. Observe `routed: <lane> -> decision - merge failed: verify full failed: pytest (rework 1/1)`.
3. Re-run the failing test unchanged — it passes.
4. Expected: a gate failure that does not reproduce is not charged against the lane's rework budget.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose verify gate fails on a check that passes when re-run unchanged when the landing is triaged then the failure is distinguished from a merit failure and does not consume the lane's rework budget with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
acceptance_criteria: Given a lane whose verify gate fails on a check that passes when re-run unchanged when the landing is triaged then the failure is distinguished from a merit failure and does not consume the lane's rework budget with tests

comments.author: niksa
comments.text:
Flake observed 2026-07-27 during the basicly-m4zv.9 build, in the worktree, on 'basicly verify --mode full': one run reported '1 failed, 1460 passed'. Seven subsequent runs of the same command in the same tree were clean (2x verify --mode full at 1461 passed, 5x pytest -q -n auto at 1461 passed), so roughly 1 in 8.

The test name is UNKNOWN and that is my process error, not a property of the flake: I piped the failing run through 'tail -12', which showed the summary block and discarded the FAILED line above it. Anyone chasing this should redirect the whole run to a file first.

Signal worth keeping: the gate's pytest check runs 'pytest -q -n auto' (basicly.toml line 92) while a bare 'uv run pytest -q' is serial and took 49s against the parallel 11s. So the flake is most likely xdist worker- or order-dependent rather than time-dependent, which narrows where to look - shared filesystem or global state between tests that land on different workers.

This is exactly the cost 55yh describes: had it hit during the landing advance instead of a hand-run, it would have spent one of the lane's two rework attempts on nothing.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text:
IDENTIFIED, same session: the flake reproduced on the basicly-m4zv.9 landing advance and it is the known upstream br clock defect, not a new one.

  RuntimeError: br update <id> --external-ref worktree:<id>:harness/<id> failed:

So the signature is the same 'updated_at cannot be before created_at' one already carried as a requirement on the Phase 6 replacement per plan section 3 principle 6. The earlier note in this thread guessed xdist worker or order dependence; that was wrong. It is a clock-resolution artifact in br's own validation when a create and an update land inside the same tick, which is why parallel runs make it more likely without being the cause.

Cost, measured rather than argued: it charged 'rework 1/2' against basicly-m4zv.9 for a defect in a dependency, with nothing in our tree to fix. That is precisely the waste this bead exists to stop, and it is now a concrete instance rather than a prediction. Nothing in the m4zv.9 diff touches the loop, br, or that test.

title: Name the violated precondition when a grant declines a ship
description:
## Context

Found by the 2026-07-31 session retro. Shipping `basicly-kjc5.58` under an active L3 grant on
`basicly-kjc5` demanded a confirm code, while two earlier beads the same session shipped with
`delegated under L3 grant`. The behaviour is CORRECT - `policy._grant_approval` requires
`lights_out_violations` to be empty for a ship, the preconditions are session-wide, and the measured
cause was `rework escalation on basicly-kjc5.56 (gate verify: 2/2)`, a wrinkle in a sibling bead
elsewhere in the epic's 55-issue session. D3 deliberately drops ship back to a human on any wrinkle.

The defect is that the refusal is **silent about why**. `_grant_approval` returns `None` and the
caller mints a confirm challenge, so the operator sees only `CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no
indication that a grant existed, covered the checkpoint, was not spend-halted, and was declined for a
specific reason in a different issue. Diagnosing it took several tool calls reading `policy.py` and
then calling `lights_out_violations` by hand.

This will recur on every child ship under any epic carrying an unresolved wrinkle, which for
`basicly-kjc5` is every remaining bead in the model-tier chain.

Related precedent for the fix's shape: the deterministic grant refusals in `_grant_refusal` already
return an explanatory string rather than a bare failure, so the module already has the idiom.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Have an active L3 grant on an epic root and a rework escalation on any child in that session.
- Run `basicly loop run <other-child> --root <epic>` to the ship checkpoint.
- Observed: `checkpoint ship: CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no reason, and nothing indicating a grant
  was present and declined. Expected: the output names the violated lights-out precondition and the
  issue it belongs to, so the operator can either fix it or knowingly relay the code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an active grant that covers ship and is not spend-halted when a lights-out precondition is
  violated elsewhere in the session then the refusal names the violated precondition and the issue it
  belongs to rather than presenting a bare confirmation request, and given no grant at all then the
  output is unchanged, with tests
acceptance_criteria: Given an active grant that covers ship and is not spend halted when a lights out precondition is violated elsewhere in the session then the refusal names the violated precondition and the issue it belongs to rather than presenting a bare confirmation request, and given no grant at all then the output is unchanged, with tests

title: Windows: deterministic rubric check test mangles the executable path via posix shlex
description:
tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code fails on windows-latest CI. evaluate_deterministic splits the check command with shlex.split (posix), and the test embeds sys.executable, which on Windows is a backslash path (<redacted:windows-drive-path>). POSIX shlex treats backslash as an escape and mangles the path, so python is not found, the check exits non-zero, and the YES assertion fails. It is deterministic on Windows, not flaky.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run pytest on Windows: tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code.
- The ok command {sys.executable} -c pass shlex-splits to a mangled path and exits non-zero.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test builds the python path with forward slashes (Path(sys.executable).as_posix()) so posix shlex.split does not mangle it and Windows still accepts the executable path; both the YES and NO assertions hold on Windows and POSIX.
- No production change: realistic authored rubric commands use bare executables or forward-slash paths; a comment records why the test uses as_posix.
- pytest stays green on all platforms.
close_reason: fixed: forward-slash executable path; windows-latest CI green (run 29640697833)

title: Speed up quality-gates CI: parallelize pytest with xdist and drop the duplicate pre-commit step
description:
The Windows quality-gates job ran ~2m47s vs ubuntu ~1m04s. Root cause: 94 subprocess-spawning CLI tests (cold python + jinja2/rich import per spawn) dominate on Windows, and CI ran the deterministic gates twice (pre-commit fast + pre-push full; full is a superset).

Fix:
1. Add pytest-xdist dev dep; run the repo pytest gate with -n auto (basicly.toml verify command). Local parallel run: 483 tests 27s -> 5.2s. Suite audited xdist-safe (all mutation in tmp_path/work_repo; REPO_ROOT reads are read-only).
2. Remove the redundant "Run pre-commit checks" CI step (full pre-push supersets it).

## Acceptance Criteria

- pytest runs in parallel via the repo gate; quality-gates.yml runs the full gate once; full suite green; Windows gate wall time materially reduced.
close_reason: Shipped: pytest-xdist -n auto via the repo gate; dropped the duplicate pre-commit CI step. Landed 27601fd, on origin/main.

title: Docs: note the br probe-leaves-tombstone trap in tool-br guidance
description:
Retro finding from the 2026-07-18 foundry-followon session (basicly-58iu). While investigating br behavior (what `br lint` flags, a `br show --json` key name), throwaway beads were created and `br delete`d. `br delete` leaves a TOMBSTONE row in `.beads/issues.jsonl`, which the harness loop's tracker-state commit then captures — so junk probe beads reach the project tracker history unless pruned. `--ephemeral` is not a workaround: ephemeral beads do not export to JSONL but `br lint` also will not lint them (`total:0`), so a lint probe needs a real bead.

Put this guidance where the next agent authoring br probes will see it: add a short note to the `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) covering the trap and the avoidance. There is no `br compact`/`purge`/`gc`; the only clean prune is `br delete <id> --hard --force` ("prunes tombstones from JSONL immediately").

## Acceptance Criteria

- The `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) gains a concise note: investigating br by creating+deleting real beads leaves tombstones the loop commits; prune with `br delete --hard`, or avoid probing the live tracker; ephemeral beads are not linted.
- Authored as YAML catalog source and projected (`basicly skills-build`/`build`); `basicly catalog lint` and the relevant `*-check` gate pass.
- Fits within the always-on budget if placed in an applies_to:[all] fragment (prefer the on-demand tool-br skill to avoid baseline growth).
close_reason: added the probe-leaves-tombstone trap note to the tool-br skill; projected to both roots; landed via base checkout after the loop escalated on a tracker-merge conflict

title: Distribute model tier guidance so an agent picks a tier by reliability
description:
## Context

Session retro 2026-07-25, from the owner correcting `docs/agent-roster-design.md`. The design shipped a three-way cheap/mid/high tier split and the rule "route to the cheapest sufficient model", plus a persona justified as "cheap tokens replacing expensive ones". Two things were wrong and the owner corrected both:

1. Providers ship three-to-four capability classes with concrete names (claude: haiku, sonnet, opus, fable - opus the workhorse, fable the designer/architect; GPT: luna, terra, sol), so a three-way generic split does not map onto anything real.
2. A cheaper model is not cheaper work. Its mistakes come back as rework dispatches, extra review cycles, bounced merges and human attention, all charged to the same change - so the cheap dispatch routinely produces the expensive outcome. The unit of cost is total tokens plus wall-clock plus human interventions per landed correct change, never the price of one dispatch.

Root cause worth fixing in prose, not just in that document: nothing the harness distributes states the unit of cost or the tier ladder, so every agent that picks a model - and the roster design itself - reasons from per-dispatch sticker price. The correction is already argued in `docs/agent-roster-design.md` section R5 (basicly-eqp6); this bead is about distributing it as catalog guidance for the agents that act on it.

Constraint to respect: the always-on baseline is at its soft cap (see basicly-c5to), so this must be a scoped fragment or a skill section, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment - or it has to pay for itself by trimming something.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a projected agent instruction surface when an agent chooses a model tier for dispatched work then the guidance states the four-tier ladder with its per-provider classes and the rule that cost is measured per landed correct change so a tier is chosen for reliability rather than sticker price with the projection gates green and the always-on budget not regressed

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`
acceptance_criteria: Given a projected agent instruction surface when an agent chooses a model tier for dispatched work then the guidance states the four-tier ladder with its per-provider classes and the rule that cost is measured per landed correct change so a tier is chosen for reliability rather than sticker price with the projection gates green and the always-on budget not regressed

title: Build the repeatable harness-vs-bare A/B eval driver and task set
description:
Follow-up from the basicly-8z52 pilot (see docs/harness-eval.md). The pilot showed the skill-injection channel measurably changes behavior on a targeted discipline at trivial token cost, but was N=1, gates-off, and partly circular. Build the repeatable A/B eval so the whole-harness claim can be re-measured on demand.

Scope:
- A small fixed, versioned task set (5-8 tasks), each targeting one harness-enforced discipline, each shipping a HIDDEN objective check the arms never see (so a skill cannot trivially satisfy the scorer).
- A thin A/B driver: run each task under Arm H (harness: skills + gates + rework loop ON) vs Arm B (bare), reusing rubrics.evaluate() for C1-C4 and policy.rework_attempts for C5. No new telemetry.
- Pin a cheap model (Haiku) on both arms via RunnerSpec.model; reserve a strong model for judging; run across >=2 agent families (Claude, Copilot).
- Report per-criterion tables + arm totals; do not collapse to one number.

The key upgrade over the pilot: turn gates + rework ON for Arm H so the deterministic-gate and rework channels (the harness's largest claimed lift) are actually measured. Shares task-set and scorer plumbing with the per-skill eval basicly-4t9z; reuses the rubric primitive basicly-0122.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A versioned fixed task set (5-8 tasks) each with a hidden objective check; a thin A/B driver reusing rubrics.evaluate for C1-C4 and policy.rework_attempts for C5 with cheap-model runner arms and a strong-model judge across >=2 agent families and gates+rework ON for the harness arm; a report of per-criterion tables and arm totals; relates to basicly-4t9z and basicly-0122 and basicly-8z52
acceptance_criteria: A versioned fixed task set (5-8 tasks) each with a hidden objective check; a thin A/B driver reusing rubrics.evaluate for C1-C4 and policy.rework_attempts for C5 with cheap-model runner arms and a strong-model judge across >=2 agent families and gates+rework ON for the harness arm; a report of per-criterion tables and arm totals; relates to basicly-4t9z and basicly-0122 and basicly-8z52

title: adopt agent-file SOTA findings: descriptive blocks, tool-time gates, deny gaps
description:
Research (2026-07-15, background agent over 9 web sources incl. Anthropic best-practices/memory/hooks docs, agents.md spec, GitHub Copilot docs, plus awesome-claude-md's 104 curated analyses and awesome-claude-code cloned locally) identified the canonical building blocks of state-of-the-art agent instruction files and control mechanisms, compared against this catalog.

Verdict: basicly is unusually STRONG on process blocks (quality-gate, git-discipline, harness-loop workflow, decision-protocol — ahead of the curated corpus) and its determinism split (git hooks + deny-list + catalog lint) is directionally validated by Anthropic's own advisory-vs-enforced distinction. It is unusually WEAK on the descriptive blocks every source puts first: (1) project overview/purpose+stack, (2) fenced build/test/lint commands — both effectively missing from the core scaffold — plus (3) no tool-time (PreToolUse) hook projection, (4) a .env Edit/Write deny gap (only Read is denied), (5) no quirks/incident category for retro output, (6) vague-adjective core-rules bullets that fail Anthropic's deletion test, (7) zero scarce-emphasis markers.

Key phrasing rules to adopt in authoring guidance: concrete+verifiable beats vague; commands in code fences are run verbatim, prose commands are improvised; pair every prohibition with an alternative; give rationale so rules generalize; emphasis is a scarce resource; every rule traces to a real incident; the deletion test ("would removing this cause mistakes? if not, cut").

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each child bead lands or is explicitly rejected with a recorded reason.
- Catalog-authoring guidance absorbs the phrasing rules (fenced commands, prohibition+alternative, rationale clauses, scarce emphasis, deletion test).

Missing only the *runner command* (see block 2) |
| 6 | **Repo etiquette / git & PR workflow** ("Repository etiquette" — Anthropic; "PR instructions" — agents.md) | Commit format, branch naming, PR conventions, hook interaction | Anthropic, agents.md, GitHub Copilot, awesome-claude-md (~22/109 quality-gate/commit blocks) | **STRONG** — `git-discipline` + `conventional-commits` skill + commit-msg hooks; the point-at-the-gate pattern here is ahead of most curated examples |
| 7 | **Boundaries / never-do list / protected paths** ("DO NOT EDIT generated files" — Pydantic; "Use pnpm — never npm or yarn" — Cloudflare) | Hard prohibitions with alternatives; generated-file and tool mandates | awesome-claude-md ~31/109; DataCamp (negation + alternative); GitHub ("prescriptive language") | **PARTIAL** — `require-explicit-confirmation` is a *confirmation* list, not a never-do list; several items are already deterministically denied in settings.json (overlap unstated). No "generated files — edit fragments instead" warning on the generated CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md themselves |
| 8 | **Verification / definition of done** ("Give Claude a check it can run" — Anthropic) | A pass/fail signal Claude runs itself; evidence over assertion | Anthropic best-practices (its top tip), awesome-claude-md quality-gate blocks, Kent Beck handoff example | **STRONG** — `quality-gate` (6 bullets; arguably the densest fragment; one of the best instances of this block found anywhere) |
| 9 | **Quirks / gotchas / environment setup** ("Quirks" — DataCamp; "document workarounds and misbehavior encountered" — GitHub; "common gotchas or non-obvious behaviors" — Anthropic) | Undocumented traps: env vars, timing, import order, platform issues | DataCamp, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic include-table, ayautomate ("gotcha-forward") | **WEAK** — `non-interactive-shell` is the only gotcha-type fragment; no per-repo quirks block, and no category for retro output to land in |
| 10 | **Workflow / methodology protocol** (plan-then-code; RIPER-5 modes; TDD contract — Kent Beck) | Phased workflow with allowed actions per phase and enforced checkpoints | Anthropic (explore→plan→implement→commit), awesome-claude-md Tier-1/2 picks (GoMall, Kent Beck) | **STRONG** — `harness-loop` with engine-enforced checkpoints; goes further than any curated example (they enforce via prose; basicly enforces via engine) |
| 11 | **Progressive-disclosure index / pointers** ("Prefer pointers to copies" — HumanLayer; "reference, don't embed" — DataCamp) | Where skills/rules/docs live; load-on-demand instead of inline | HumanLayer, DataCamp, Anthropic memory docs (skills vs rules vs CLAUDE.md decision), Copilot `applyTo` | **COVERED** — `use`, `claude-defaults`, `copilot-defaults`, `catalog-authoring`; skills carry tool knowledge |
| 12 | **Escalation / decision protocol** | When to act autonomously vs stop and ask | Weakest external evidence — appears only implicitly (plan mode, RIPER-5 mode permissions). Largely a basicly original; flag as opinion-supported, not SOTA-corroborated | **COVERED** — `decision-protocol` (basicly is ahead of the corpus here) |

---

## 2. Top 10 phrasing rules (best vs worst)

1. **Concrete and verifiable beats vague intent.** Best: "Use 2-space indentation, no semicolons, single quotes." Worst: "Format code properly." (Anthropic memory docs + DataCamp, verbatim-corroborated.)
2. **Put runnable commands in code fences.** "A command inside a code fence is something Claude will run verbatim. A command written in a sentence is a suggestion it might improvise on." (DataCamp.) Worst: prose like "run the linter before committing" with no command.
3. **Pair every prohibition with an alternative.** Best: "Never use `--legacy-peer-deps`; resolve conflicts by updating the package." Worst: negation-only rules that leave the agent stuck. (DataCamp; basicly already does this well: "…bypassing hooks — fix the failing gate instead.")
4. **Give rationale so the rule generalizes.** Best: "Never force push. This rewrites shared history and is unrecoverable for collaborators." Worst: bare "Never force push." (DataCamp.)
5. **Emphasis is a scarce resource.** Anthropic: "You can tune instructions by adding emphasis (e.g., 'IMPORTANT' or 'YOU MUST')" — but "if every rule is marked important, the emphasis becomes invisible" (DataCamp). Worst: bolding everything. (Note: basicly currently uses *zero* emphasis markers — headroom exists.)
6. **Strict imperative mandates for critical tool choices, with reasoning.** Best: "Use `pnpm` — never use npm or yarn" (Cloudflare); "UV over pip, basedpyright over mypy" with stated rationale (Pydantic). Worst: "use appropriate tooling."
7. **Point at the gate, don't restate it.** Best: "Commits are gated by commit-msg hooks — use the `conventional-commits` skill" (basicly's own pattern, matching HumanLayer/DataCamp "reference, don't embed"). Worst: restating linter rules the formatter already enforces.
8. **Only repo-specific content.** "Every line should answer 'what does Claude need to know about THIS repo?'" (ayautomate). Worst: "TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript"; "write clean code" (Anthropic's explicit exclude list).
9. **Every rule traces to a real incident.** "Every rule should trace back to a real incident, not a hypothetical one" (DataCamp); identity-guard.py's docstring ("the exact failure this repo hit") is a textbook instance. Worst: speculative edge-case rules that "help in narrow situations and hurt in the majority of sessions."
10. **The deletion test.** "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it" (Anthropic + DataCamp, identical phrasing). Corollary anti-pattern: "If Claude keeps ignoring a rule, don't add more words around it" — the file is too long. Sources converge on <200 lines (Anthropic), <300/"under sixty" (HumanLayer), 100-400 (ayautomate); GitHub caps Copilot instructions at "no longer than 2 pages."

---

## 3. Determinism ledger

The operating principle under test — *everything that doesn't have to be suggestive should be deterministic and gated* — is **directly validated by primary sources**: Anthropic's memory doc says "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead," and its managed-settings table splits "technical enforcement" (settings) from "behavioral guidance" (CLAUDE.md). Anthropic's own steering post is "organized around deterministic-versus-probabilistic control" (awesome-claude-code, From Anthropic section). awesome-claude-md's meta-lesson: "enforce standards through tooling rather than relying on developer discipline."

| Concern | Recommended mechanism | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Formatting, import order, lint | Formatter + pre-commit/PostToolUse hook; **never prose** | HumanLayer, DataCamp, awesome-claude-md (unanimous) |
| Commit message format | commit-msg hook | awesome-claude-md quality-gate examples; basicly practice |
| Protected files (.env, lockfiles, generated, migrations) | PreToolUse hook (exit 2) or `permissions.deny` | Anthropic hooks guide (protect-files.sh example, "Write a hook that blocks writes to the migrations folder") |
| Destructive commands (rm -rf, force-push, DROP TABLE) | `permissions.deny` + PreToolUse guardrail script; a whole tool ecosystem exists (Claude Code Safety Net, Safety Guard "born from a real incident", GouvernAI "auto-approve safe, gate risky, block dangerous", Node9) | Anthropic hooks guide (block-rm-rf.sh, "dropping tables is not allowed" exit-2 example); awesome-claude-code Security category |
| Actions that must happen every time | Hooks: "for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions. Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic" | Anthropic best-practices, verbatim |
| Definition-of-done checks | Stop hook ("blocks the turn from ending until it passes") or CI | Anthropic best-practices |
| Timed/positional instructions ("before every commit") | Hook, not CLAUDE.md: "if the instruction must run at a specific point… write it as a hook instead" | Anthropic memory docs, verbatim |
| Org-wide policy | Managed settings `permissions.deny` / `sandbox.enabled` for enforcement; managed CLAUDE.md only for guidance | Anthropic memory docs table |
| Secret leakage | Scanner in git hooks/CI (Agent Guard), not prose | awesome-claude-code Security |
| Autonomy blast radius | OS sandbox / Docker isolation ("give the agent a cage, not your keys" — Cleat) + `--allowedTools` scoping | Anthropic best-practices, awesome-claude-code |
| Instruction-file quality itself | Lint it: agnix (linter/LSP for CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/hooks), Schliff (8-dimension scorer) — validates basicly's `catalog-lint` approach | awesome-claude-code Linting category |
| What stays prose | Judgment calls: architecture rationale, escalation rules, review philosophy, style *deltas*, gotchas — anything requiring context-sensitive judgment ("prompt-based hooks" exist for the middle ground) | Anthropic hooks guide |

---

## 4. Prioritized recommendations for basicly's catalog

1. **(High) Add a first-class `project-overview` + `commands` core scaffold.** The two most-corroborated blocks (purpose/stack, fenced commands) are the weakest in basicly. `project-defaults` is a thin local overlay with no "why" and an explicit "no build/test command" placeholder. Concrete: make `basicly init`/docs require a per-repo `project-overview` fragment (purpose in 1-2 lines, stack with versions, entry points, pointer to `docs/architecture.md`) and a `commands` fragment whose body is fenced command groups (`uv sync`, `uv run pytest`, `basicly catalog-lint`, hook build). Body sketch for commands: "```\nuv run pytest              # full suite\nuv run pytest tests/x.py   # single file\nbasicly catalog-lint       # catalog format gate\n```". Heed the `/doctor` caveat: pointers to architecture docs, not embedded layouts.
2. **(High) Close the deny-list gap on `.env` and demote confirmed-deterministic prose.** settings.json denies `Read(.env*)` but **not `Edit`/`Write`** on them — the confirmation-list item "editing … `.env*`" is enforceable today (`Edit(.env*)`, `Write(.env*)` deny rules, or a projected protect-files PreToolUse hook). Then annotate `require-explicit-confirmation` to state which items are hard-denied (force-push, `--no-verify`, `rm -rf`, `reset --hard`) so prose carries rationale, and only the genuinely judgment-y items (dependency changes, CI/CD edits, new network calls) remain suggestive.
3. **(High) Project agent-native hooks, not just git hooks.** basicly's targets project markdown + git hooks; git hooks gate only at commit time. Anthropic's model gates at *tool* time (PreToolUse) and *turn end* (Stop). Concrete: add a `targets/*.yaml` output that renders a hooks manifest into `.claude/settings.json` (and Copilot equivalents as they mature) — starting with a protect-files guard for generated outputs (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `copilot-instructions.md` — "DO NOT EDIT generated files" is a Tier-1 curated pattern (Pydantic), and basicly's equivalent rule currently lives only in `catalog-authoring` prose).
4. **(Medium) Add a `quirks` fragment category and wire the retro to it.** DataCamp's "every rule traces to a real incident" is exactly `self-improvement-retro`'s philosophy, but retro proposals have no natural landing zone for repo-specific traps (the identity-guard hook's origin story is the pattern). A `quirks/` category with one-incident-one-bullet discipline completes the loop.
5. **(Medium) Prune `core-rules` against the exclude-list.** Several bullets fail the deletion test per Anthropic's exclude table ("self-evident practices like 'write clean code'"): "Prioritize correctness over speed" and "Prefer explicit, readable solutions over clever ones" are vague-adjective rules the model follows anyway. The generated file is 116 lines (healthy, under the 200-line consensus) — but the just-completed size-cap commit suggests budget pressure; these are the cheapest cuts.
6. **(Low) Introduce scarce emphasis.** Zero `IMPORTANT`/`YOU MUST` markers exist across the catalog. Anthropic explicitly endorses sparse emphasis for adherence tuning; consider it for exactly one rule per projection (candidate: the never-bypass-gates rule, which prose must still carry for agents other than Claude Code).
7. **(Low, flag-as-opinion) Add rationale clauses to bare prohibitions.** e.g. secure-coding's "Never commit secrets" bullets already carry alternatives; `require-explicit-confirmation`'s "Force-push, history rewrite" line would generalize better with a one-clause "rewrites shared history" rationale (single-source DataCamp claim, uncorroborated by primary docs).

**Overall verdict:** basicly's fragment set is unusually strong on process blocks (verification, git etiquette, workflow protocol, decision rules — better than the curated corpus) and unusually weak on the *descriptive* blocks every source puts first (what the project is, how to build/test it, where things live). Its determinism split is directionally correct and ahead of most examples (git-hook gates + deny-list + catalog lint), with the two concrete deterministic gaps being tool-time hooks and the `.env` write hole.

---

## 5. Sources

| Source | Credibility |
|---|---|
| Anthropic — Claude Code best practices (code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) | Primary/official; the include/exclude table and hooks-vs-advisory distinction are the strongest evidence in this report. |
| Anthropic — Memory docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) | Primary/official; canonical on locations, imports, rules, size (<200 lines), and the enforcement split (managed settings vs CLAUDE.md). |
| Anthropic — Hooks guide (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide) | Primary/official; canonical on PreToolUse blocking (exit 2 / JSON deny), protect-files and block-rm-rf examples. |
| agents.md spec | Primary for the AGENTS.md convention (60k+ repos, 20+ tools); deliberately minimal — suggests sections, mandates nothing. |
| GitHub Copilot custom-instructions docs | Primary/official for copilot-instructions.md, `applyTo` scoping, 2-page cap, validated-commands dos/don'ts. |
| github.com/josix/awesome-claude-md (cloned, 104 analyses read via subagent) | Curated secondary with an explicit 100-point rubric; analyses are third-party interpretations, not the source files themselves — good for pattern frequency, weaker for verbatim phrasing. |
| github.com/hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code (cloned, README + resources CSV) | Curated secondary; its Security/Linting/From-Anthropic categories evidence the deterministic-controls ecosystem; entry descriptions are editorial. |
| DataCamp — "Writing the best CLAUDE.md" | Solid secondary tutorial; consistent with primary docs; several claims (code-fence-verbatim, incident-traceability) are single-source opinion. |
| Braincuber — "Writing best CLAUDE.md complete guide" | **Low independent value: near-verbatim mirror of the DataCamp piece** (identical section list, deletion test, negation advice). Treated as one source, not two. |
| ayautomate — "Best CLAUDE.md examples" | Secondary listicle; useful example inventory and the 100-400-line claim; no determinism coverage; treat length claim as opinion. |
| HumanLayer — "Writing a good CLAUDE.md" | High-quality practitioner essay; instruction-budget argument (~150-200 instructions) and "pointers over copies" are its distinctive, widely cited contributions. |

title: core scaffold: project-overview and fenced commands fragments
description:
The two most-corroborated blocks (every source puts them first) are missing from the core scaffold: a project-overview fragment (purpose in 1-2 lines, stack with versions, entry points, pointer to architecture docs — NOT an embedded directory map, per Anthropic /doctor trim guidance) and a commands fragment whose body is fenced, verbatim-runnable command groups (setup/test/single-test/lint). install should scaffold per-repo overlay stubs for both so every consumer starts with them.

## Design

Content is inherently per-repo, so these land as install-scaffolded overlay stubs (written once when absent, never overwritten — same contract as tasks.json/basicly-gates.yml), created as status: draft so placeholder text never pollutes projections (planner filters to active); the consumer fills them in and flips to active. This repo dogfoods by authoring real, active versions in its own overlay.

## Acceptance Criteria

- basicly install scaffolds .basicly-local/fragments/user/project/project-overview.fragment.yaml and .basicly-local/fragments/user/commands/commands.fragment.yaml when absent, with draft status and a fill-me structure (overview: purpose, stack, entry points, docs pointer; commands: fenced setup/test/single-test/lint groups).
- Existing files at those paths are never overwritten on re-install.
- Scaffolded stubs load as valid fragments (catalog-lint passes with them present) and, being draft, do not change projections until activated.
- Unit tests cover: scaffold-when-absent, no-overwrite, stub validity.
- Dogfood: this repo's overlay gains real active project-overview and commands fragments; projections regenerated; all checks green.

title: project agent-native tool-time hooks (protect generated files)
description:
Git hooks gate only at commit time; Anthropic's model gates at tool time (PreToolUse, exit 2 blocks) and turn end (Stop). Add a projection of agent-native hooks into .claude/settings.json, starting with a protect-files guard for generated outputs (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, rules/instructions files, projected skills) — the do-not-edit-generated-files rule currently lives only in prose. Tier-1 curated pattern (Pydantic's DO NOT EDIT blocks).

## Design

- New stdlib-only script .basicly/core/hooks/protect-generated.py: reads the PreToolUse JSON payload from stdin, extracts tool_input.file_path, and exits 2 (block, stderr shown to the model with the edit-the-source alternative) when the target file carries a 'Generated by ... basicly' marker in its first lines or is the generated manifest json; fails open on malformed input or missing files.
- hooks.yaml entries gain an optional manager field (default git); the new hook is manager claude, stage pretooluse. Git-side rendering (pre-commit config, stage installation) filters to manager git.
- claude_settings.py gains merge/check functions that project manager-claude hooks into the hooks.PreToolUse section of the committed .claude/settings.json (matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit), preserving all consumer keys and any foreign hooks; idempotent by managed command match.
- hooks-build applies the settings projection; hooks-check reports drift.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Editing a marker-carrying generated file through Edit/Write is blocked by the hook script (exit 2) with a message naming the catalog source workflow; normal files pass; malformed payloads fail open.
- basicly hooks-build writes the PreToolUse wiring into .claude/settings.json without disturbing existing settings; re-running is a no-op; hooks-check flags a removed or altered managed entry.
- pre-commit config and git stage installation are unchanged by the new manager field (git hooks keep working; agent hooks never reach pre-commit).
- Unit tests cover the script verdicts, the settings merge/check, and the manager filtering.
- Dogfood: this repo's .claude/settings.json gains the wiring via hooks-build; piping a synthetic PreToolUse payload for CLAUDE.md into the script blocks it.

title: Add install provenance/state tracking (.basicly/state/install.json)
description:
Record installed catalog version + provenance so upgrades can be reasoned about and `basicly check` can report drift (architecture §9). Written by `basicly install` when it materializes the bundled catalog into a consumer repo (skipped in the authoring repo, where core is its own source). Snapshot the on-disk core state right after materialize, so a later hash mismatch means a hand-edit — the provenance basis the core-sync task basicly-zrj.12.2 needs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `basicly install` in a consumer repo writes `.basicly/state/install.json` (path follows the configured core root) recording: schema version, basicly version, install timestamp, and a per-file sha256 map of the managed core as materialized.
- A second install refreshes the timestamp/version and re-snapshots; the file is valid JSON with a stable schema.
- `basicly check` surfaces provenance drift as advisory notes: core files modified or removed relative to the recorded snapshot, and an installed-vs-current basicly version mismatch. Exit code contract of `check` is unchanged by these notes.
- The authoring repo (core == bundled source) writes no state file and reports no provenance notes.
- Unit/integration tests cover: state written on install, re-install refresh, modified-core drift note, and authoring-repo skip.
