title: Reopen projecting subagents to the copilot agents surface with new facts
description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-31. `src/basicly/agents.py:24-46` records that the non-claude subagent roots were
"weighed and declined, so re-opening this needs new facts, not a fresh reading". This bead brings the
new facts, gathered from live authoritative docs at the owner's direction after basicly-kjc5.58 landed.

The declined reason for `.github/agents/*.md` was that it is "the same markdown format but a separate
root", and basicly-ajq "kept one root and bought portability in the content instead". The supporting
claim was that VS Code parses the Claude subagent format natively - which is still TRUE and is now
confirmed in VS Code's own docs: "VS Code also detects `.md` files in the `.claude/agents` folder,
following the Claude sub-agents format".

## The new facts

1. **VS Code is not the only copilot surface, and the others do not read `.claude/agents`.** The GitHub
   Copilot **cloud agent** reads `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root `agents/`), and
   Copilot CLI is documented on the same custom-agent surface. So our subagents do not exist at all for
   the cloud agent - the single-root decision covers VS Code only, which is narrower than the comment
   reads.
2. **Copilot custom agents DO support a `tools` allowlist**, so the objection that killed the codex root
   (basicly-crkl: no `tools` equivalent, therefore a silently lost read-only guarantee) does **not**
   apply here. The guarantee is expressible.
3. **Copilot supports a per-agent `model`**, which is the whole point of basicly-a3yi. Without this
   root, a declared tier can never reach copilot at all.
4. Copilot's frontmatter is a **superset** in places (`target`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`,
   `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`) and its body cap is 30000 chars, which
   `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already enforces.

## The real costs, stated honestly

- **Tool names differ and the sources disagree.** VS Code's doc example is `["read","search","edit"]`;
  community material shows `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github`. Claude's are `Read`/`Grep`/`Glob`/`Bash`.
  So this needs a pinned, reviewed tool-name mapping plus a rule for a Claude tool with no copilot
  equivalent - and mapping wrongly would weaken the read-only posture check (`WRITE_TOOLS`), which is
  exactly the class of lost guarantee basicly-crkl refused. This is the bead's main risk, not the format.
- `agents-check` needs the `--all-default-roots` treatment `skills-check` already has, or a second root
  drifts unnoticed.
- A second root doubles the generated-file surface for `protect-generated` and the GENERATED_MARKER.
- No always-on cost: subagents are on-demand files.

## Decide, do not assume

The decision is whether the copilot cloud agent and CLI are real consumers for this distribution. If
they are, this root is required and blocks the copilot half of basicly-a3yi. If they are not, say so in
the comment so the next reader does not re-derive it - and then a declared tier is claude-only by
policy, which should be written down rather than left implicit.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `src/basicly/cli.py`, `tests/test_agents.py`, `.basicly/core/targets/`.
acceptance_criteria: Given the copilot custom agent surface when the decision is recorded then either subagents project to that root with a pinned reviewed tool name mapping that preserves the read only posture check and agents-check covers every root, or the decision to stay claude only is written down with its reason so a declared tier is documented as claude only by policy, with tests where code lands

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: TOOL-NAME VOCABULARIES CONFIRMED INCOMPATIBLE 2026-07-31, from the two authoritative references the owner supplied (code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference and code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/ai-features-cheat-sheet#_chat-tools). This upgrades the tool-name mapping from a cost to the bead's central risk. CLAUDE CODE: flat CapitalCase strings, and the doc states they are 'the exact strings you use in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers' - Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent, WebFetch, Skill, TodoWrite and ~40 more. COPILOT / VS CODE: hash-prefixed and NAMESPACED INTO SETS. Sets: #agent #browser #edit #execute #read #search #web. Individual tools are set-slash-name, e.g. #read/readFile, #search/textSearch, #search/fileSearch, #search/codebase, #execute/runInTerminal, #edit/editFiles, #edit/createFile, #web/fetch, #agent/runSubagent. The doc states these are the exact configuration strings, not display names. MAPPING FOR THE TOOLS WE ACTUALLY SHIP (all three agents: test-runner [Read Grep Glob Bash], code-reviewer [Read Grep Glob Bash], security-auditor [Read Grep Glob]): Read -> #read/readFile; Grep -> #search/textSearch; Glob -> #search/fileSearch; Bash -> #execute/runInTerminal. THE SET TRAP, which is the security finding: #read is NOT 'read a file' - it is a GROUP that also contains #read/problems, #read/terminalLastCommand, #read/terminalSelection and notebook readers; #execute also contains createAndRunTask, getTerminalOutput, runNotebookCell and testFailure; #edit also contains createDirectory and editNotebook. So the natural-looking mapping Read -> #read silently WIDENS the grant. Any mapping must target the set-slash-name leaf, never the bare set, and #edit must never appear for an agent our WRITE_TOOLS check certified read-only. A THIRD VOCABULARY EXISTS: copilot CLI's own preToolUse hook payload reported toolName 'bash' and 'task' - lowercase and unnamespaced - matching neither published list, while .github/agents/*.agent.md is shared between VS Code and the CLI via the target field. So the same tools: array is read by surfaces that may not agree on the vocabulary. SUSPECTED SILENT ACCEPTANCE - the decisive open question: a probe agent declaring tools: ['read'] (not a documented config string; #read is) loaded and RAN on copilot CLI with no complaint. Claude Code by contrast documents that if no entry resolves to a tool the subagent 'usually fails to launch with an error naming the entries'. If copilot ignores an unrecognised entry and falls back to its default toolset, then our mandatory-allowlist guarantee and the read-only posture validation are VACUOUS on copilot - a lost guarantee, the same class of objection that declined the codex root in basicly-crkl. This must be settled empirically before any copilot projection ships. An investigation is running to confirm loudly-vs-silently.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: CORRECTION 2026-07-31 - my previous comment on this bead was WRONG on its central claim and on the security concern. Measured investigation, sources: docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/custom-agents-configuration and code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference. (1) GITHUB DOES NOT NAME ITS TOOLS DIFFERENTLY. It publishes an alias table that accepts Claude's PascalCase names as first-class compatible aliases: execute accepts shell/Bash/powershell; read accepts Read/NotebookRead; edit accepts Edit/MultiEdit/Write/NotebookEdit; search accepts Grep/Glob; agent accepts custom-agent/Task; web accepts WebSearch/WebFetch; todo accepts TodoWrite. All aliases are case-insensitive, both a comma-separated string and a YAML array are accepted, and unset defaults to all tools. This is deliberate claude-compatibility engineering, like the .claude/skills support. So the earlier claim that a mapping is required is wrong - our existing names already work. GitHub publishes no enumerated tool list, which is itself worth recording. The VS Code cheat sheet's hash-prefixed namespaced names and tool SETS are a THIRD vocabulary for VS Code chat, and the CLI's internal names are a fourth (measured: view, grep, glob, bash, create, edit, skill, sql). Do not merge them. The deepwiki/awesome-copilot list (codebase, terminal, edit, github) matches no vendor source and should be discarded. (2) COPILOT ENFORCES THE ALLOWLIST - measured deterministically, not judged: copilot --log-level debug writes the model request payload, so the actual granted tool schemas are observable. tools ['NotAToolAtAll'] granted only skill+sql; tools [Read Grep Glob Bash] granted view+grep+glob+bash+read_bash+stop_bash+list_bash+skill+sql. Behaviourally the nonsense agent refused both WRITE and SHELL and created no file. (3) THE FEARED LOST GUARANTEE DOES NOT MATERIALISE. An unrecognised entry is dropped with no error and no warning (unlike claude code, which refuses to launch and names the unresolved entries) - but it does NOT fall back to grant-all: an all-unrecognised list resolved to zero requested tools. Our four shipped names all resolve and none resolves to edit or create. The residual risk is functional, not security: a typo yields a near-useless agent rather than a loud failure. (4) REAL SMALLER FINDINGS, all measured: skill and sql are granted UNCONDITIONALLY and cannot be suppressed by our allowlist, so a read-only agent on copilot always holds two tools we never declared (sql writes to a per-session SQLite db, not the repo). Bash yields FOUR tools - bash plus read_bash/stop_bash/list_bash - same capability class, wider surface. NotebookEdit alone resolves to create AND edit, i.e. general filesystem write, so the narrowest notebook write tool on claude becomes full write on copilot - latent, since we do not ship it and WRITE_TOOLS would reject it in a read-only agent. Alias expansion is not uniform: Glob did NOT pull in grep, so a name with a 1:1 CLI counterpart maps narrowly while one without falls back to the broader primary set. (5) THE FINDING THAT MOST CHANGES THIS BEAD: the copilot CLI DOES discover .claude/agents/*.md - measured, a probe agent placed there appeared in the roster and its comma-string allowlist resolved correctly. So our shipped subagents are ALREADY live on copilot today. But GitHub documents only .github/agents/ and ~/.copilot/agents/ for agents; .claude/ is documented only for skills. So this bead's justification shifts: it is no longer 'make copilot work' but 'stop depending on undocumented discovery that no gate would catch if it regressed'. Cheap mitigation available at zero credit cost: copilot --agent <bogus-name> -p x errors and prints the discovered roster without an AI call, so a load assertion is testable for free. Investigation cost 25.29 AI credits over 4 dispatches.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: OWNER DECISION 2026-07-31: take the FIRST branch of the AC - project subagents to the copilot agents root. Do not re-litigate. Reasoning that survived the correction: (1) the copilot CLOUD agent reads .github/agents/<name>.agent.md and our subagents do not exist for it at all, so the old single-root decision only ever covered VS Code; (2) the copilot CLI does discover .claude/agents but that is UNDOCUMENTED behaviour we are silently depending on - GitHub documents only .github/agents/ and ~/.copilot/agents/; (3) copilot custom agents support a tools allowlist so the read-only posture check IS expressible, which removes the objection that killed the codex root in basicly-crkl; (4) decisive one - copilot cannot intercept a spawn (repo-level hooks never fire, measured across three probes), so static per-surface emission is copilot's ONLY path and basicly-a3yi needs a root with a documented model slot to emit into. IMPORTANT correction to this bead's own premise: NO tool-name mapping is needed. GitHub publishes an alias table that accepts Claude PascalCase names as first-class and matches case-insensitively (read <- Read/NotebookRead, search <- Grep/Glob, execute <- shell/Bash/powershell, edit <- Edit/MultiEdit/Write/NotebookEdit, agent <- custom-agent/Task, web <- WebSearch/WebFetch, todo <- TodoWrite). An unknown name is dropped silently but fails SAFE - no grant-all fallback. So the AC's pinned reviewed tool name mapping is simpler than filed: pin the alias table as reviewed data and assert our declared names resolve, rather than authoring a translation layer. Accepted cost: a second projected root in the drift gate, and basicly install starts writing .github/agents/ which is consumer-visible and needs a changelog entry.

title: loop supervise hides its own progress when stdout is a pipe
description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

The run was piped through `tee` to a log so it could be followed live. For roughly twelve minutes
the only output was the lanes' own subprocess noise — markdownlint summaries and pytest tracebacks
from their pre-commit hooks. Not one `session:`, `adopted:`, `dispatch:` or `routed:` line
appeared until the process exited, at which point the whole orchestration history arrived at once.

Cause: `_cmd_loop_supervise` reports with plain `print`, and Python block-buffers stdout when it is
not a TTY. The lanes' output is not buffered because it comes from child processes writing to an
inherited file descriptor, so the operator sees everything *except* the thing the supervisor is
supposed to tell them.

This is the same blind spot basicly-jr0l.10 records for spend, generalized to every line the
supervisor prints. It matters because a long headless run is exactly the case where an operator
pipes to a log or a pager, and because it defeats "watch the run and intervene early" as a
mitigation for cost: the lanes had already finished and cost 3.36M tokens before the first
orchestration line was visible.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `basicly loop supervise <root> | tee run.log` with at least one lane that takes minutes.
2. Observe `run.log` and the terminal while it runs: hook and test output from the lanes appears immediately, supervisor lines do not.
3. Wait for exit — every supervisor line appears at once.
4. Expected: each supervisor line is visible as it happens, piped or not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given loop supervise running with stdout attached to a pipe rather than a terminal when the supervisor prints a session or dispatch or routed line then that line is observable before the process exits with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
acceptance_criteria: Given loop supervise running with stdout attached to a pipe rather than a terminal when the supervisor prints a session or dispatch or routed line then that line is observable before the process exits with tests

title: Research spike: is basicly measurably better than a standalone agent harness
description:
Objectively test whether driving work through the basicly harness (the loop, distributed skills, deterministic gates, worktree isolation) produces higher-quality completed work than a standalone Claude Code or GitHub Copilot session with no basicly harness. Today this is asserted, not measured.

Design a low-token-cost evaluation:
- A small fixed task set (a handful of representative, deterministic coding tasks with objective pass criteria).
- Run each task both ways: with the basicly harness vs a bare agent, ideally across more than one agent (Claude Code, Copilot) to avoid single-agent bias.
- Score on completion quality, correctness (tests/gates), and rework/iterations.

Minimize token usage as a hard design constraint: use faster/cheaper models (e.g. Haiku) for the runner passes and reserve a stronger model only for judging; keep the task set small and deterministic; reuse existing signals rather than re-instrumenting - the run-record health signal (basicly-y886) and the rubric eval (basicly-0122). Relate to basicly-4t9z (skill evals), which measures per-skill behavioral lift; this bead is the whole-harness question, not per-skill.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A documented A/B methodology (harness vs no-harness) over a small fixed task set, with an explicit token-minimization strategy (cheap models for the runner passes, strong model only for scoring, small deterministic tasks, reuse of run-records/health and rubric signals).
- A scoring rubric covering completion, correctness, and rework, with objective pass criteria per task.
- A pilot run with results and a recommendation on whether basicly measurably helps and whether to make this a repeatable eval (and if so, what to build). References basicly-4t9z and basicly-0122.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Pilot result (docs/harness-eval.md): skill-injection channel measurably shifted behavior on the targeted discipline - Arm H (skills prepended) 4/4 vs Arm B (bare) 3/4, the delta on C4 test-discipline (H stubbed subprocess + regression tests; B wrote real-git integration tests). Equal correctness on a hidden objective check (C2 tie), at ~32k Haiku tokens. Caveats: N=1, one agent/model, gates+rework off, and the C4 win is partly circular (H was told to stub). Recommendation: YES make it repeatable but scoped - filed basicly-7bur to build a fixed task set with HIDDEN objective checks + a thin A/B driver reusing rubrics.evaluate and the rework counter, cheap-model arms + strong judge, and gates+rework ON for the harness arm (the channel this pilot deferred and where the largest lift lives). Sibling to basicly-4t9z; reuses basicly-0122.

title: loop advance from a linked worktree should refuse the merge/ship transition
description:
Field incident shipping basicly-yzyd.1: running 'basicly loop advance' with cwd inside a loop worktree (not the base checkout) made the merge fail ('merge must run from the base checkout ... currently on harness/<name>') yet the ship-checkpoint approval and teardown still proceeded, leaving the child CLOSED but UNMERGED with its commit stranded on the harness branch. The engine should detect it is running from a linked worktree (or that 'main' is not the checked-out base) and refuse the merge/ship transition with a clear error, instead of approving-and-stranding. Also: worktree cleanup --force did not remove the orphaned .git/basicly-worktrees/<name>.json session record once the branch was already deleted, and that stale record counts toward the worktree concurrency cap. Recovery used: git rebase main harness/<name> + git merge --ff-only + git branch -d + rm the stale session json.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Provision a leaf worktree via the loop and cd into it (the linked worktree)
2. From inside the worktree, run 'basicly loop advance <id>' at the build or ship phase
3. Observe the merge fail on base-checkout assertion while ship approval/teardown still closes the bead, stranding the commit on harness/<name>

## Acceptance Criteria

* loop advance refuses the build and ship transitions when run from a linked worktree (git-dir != git-common-dir), returning a graceful blocked result that names the base checkout and mutates no tracker/worktree state
* worktree cleanup drops the session record when the branch is already gone, so no orphaned .json counts toward the concurrency cap
* regression tests cover the linked-worktree refusal and the already-deleted-branch cleanup

title: A hook script change cannot pass the landing verify from a worktree
description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-31 while landing basicly-m0p1, which edits `.basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py`. The
build->verify landing failed with `projection-hooks`:

    Stale hook projection detected. Run `basicly hooks-build` to sync hooks.
      .basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py: differs from catalog

The projection was not stale. `hooks.check_hooks` compares `_catalog_hooks_dir()` - the hooks
directory of the **installed** basicly package - against `repo_root / core_hooks_dir`, and skips the
comparison entirely when the two resolve to the same path. In this repo basicly is installed editable
from the base checkout, so `_catalog_hooks_dir()` resolves to
`<base>/.basicly/core/hooks`. The loop's landing verify runs with `repo_root` set to the **lane's
worktree**. So the check compares the pre-merge BASE copy against the post-change WORKTREE copy and
reports a difference that is the change itself.

Measured: base copy md5 `97d34d0e...`, worktree copy md5 `389ad855...`, and calling
`check_hooks(<worktree>, Path(".basicly/core/hooks"))` from the base interpreter reproduces the single
mismatch exactly.

Consequence: **any change to a hook script is unlandable through the loop.** It is not "landed by its
own pre-merge version" (the documented `merge.py`/`loop.py`/`verify.py` trap) - it structurally cannot
pass, and it consumes the rework budget on each attempt (observed at 1/2 after one try).

**The dangerous part, and the reason this is P1 rather than an annoyance:** the failure message tells
the operator to run `basicly hooks-build`. In a worktree that copies the base's OLD script over the
new one, silently reverting the work while turning the gate green. An agent following the message
faithfully destroys the change and reports success.

Note the check is only meaningful for a CONSUMER repo, where `.basicly/core/` is materialised from the
wheel and can genuinely drift. In the dev repo `src` and `dst` are the same directory, so the content
comparison is skipped and the gate has no signal to give - which is why it passes from base and fails
only from a worktree.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Provision a worktree for any bead and edit any file under `.basicly/core/hooks/`.
- Commit it on the harness branch, then run `basicly loop run <id> --root <id>` from base.
- Observed: `projection-hooks` fails naming the edited script as differing from catalog, the merge is
  rolled back, and rework increments. Expected: the check compares like with like - or is skipped -
  when the repo under verification is a linked worktree of the checkout the package is installed from.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a harness worktree whose hook source differs from the base checkout it was branched from when
  the landing verify runs the projection-hooks check then the check does not report the change itself
  as drift and the landing proceeds, and given a consumer repo whose materialised hooks genuinely
  differ from the installed catalog then it still fails, and the failure message no longer advises a
  command that would revert the change when run in a worktree, with tests
acceptance_criteria: Given a harness worktree whose hook source differs from the base checkout it was branched from when the landing verify runs the projection hooks check then the check does not report the change itself as drift and the landing proceeds, and given a consumer repo whose materialised hooks genuinely differ from the installed catalog then it still fails, and the failure message no longer advises a command that would revert the change when run in a worktree, with tests

title: wait-meter tests budgeted 5s for two real br calls, so a loaded machine fails the push
description:
tests/test_integration_wait.py asserted 'waited_s <= _WAITED_S + _SLACK_S' with _SLACK_S=5. The fixture pins policy._now to time.time()+600, so the recorded interval is 600 plus however long the two real br round-trips take. The upper bound therefore budgeted five seconds for two subprocess invocations.

On a loaded full-suite run (15m37s wall) they took nine, producing 'assert 609 <= (600 + 5)' and failing the pre-push gate for a defect that did not exist. Three test_integration_dor_scaffold setup errors in the same run were xdist contention, not real - that file passes 15/15 in 40s on its own.

Fixed by taking the overhead from time.monotonic() around the two calls and allowing it explicitly, per .claude/rules/platform-hermetic-tests.md ('wait for the condition, never for a duration'). The bound keeps its power: with ~1s elapsed the ceiling is ~606s, so a mis-zoned stamp hours off still fails.

Found while pinning br to 0.2.16 (basicly-o7z5); unrelated to that change.
close_reason: Two defects, both shipped: the wait-meter tolerance now comes from a monotonic clock (177109f), and pytest workers are capped at 4 so br's machine-global write lock stops timing out (dea43cf). The br-backed integration files went from 10 errors in 3m47s under -n auto to 33 passed in 2m26s. Push landed: 52c1893..dea43cf.

title: Phase 4 relieve the always-on layer
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 4. P1 if 1a shows a cliff, P2 if it shows a slope - filed at P2 pending 1a. Depends on 1a for urgency and 2a as adjacent work. Size 2-3 sessions.

Cheaper than the design documents assume because the mechanism is already built. Verified 2026-07-26 at c175c1a: the path-scoped tier is fully wired (schema.py:153 has_scope/exclude_scoped, planner.py:76, rule_md.j2 for both claude and codex) and zero of the 19 fragments declare a scope. Baseline measured at 7014/7209/7343 chars for AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/copilot-instructions.md, about 1070 words each against a 9000 soft cap.

Watch the asymmetry: scoping removes a fragment from the Claude and Copilot baselines but not from the Codex one, which inlines scoped fragments because our scopes are globs and nested AGENTS.md is directory-based. A claim of cutting the baseline must name the family, and scoping is a deliberate removal from the github.com Copilot surface - a guarantee change per fragment, not a refactor.
acceptance_criteria: Given the always-on layer is relieved when the baselines are re-measured then they are measurably smaller on two of three agent families and the 1a recall test re-run shows improved recall and no declared scope matches nothing

title: Audit every always-on line for hook glob and no-op
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 4 step 1. Depends on 1a for its urgency.

Audit every baseline line against three questions:
- is this really a hook - can a git hook or a verify check enforce it instead of asking;
- can I write a glob for it - does it belong in the path-scoped tier rather than always-on;
- does it change behaviour versus the default at all.

Expect all three to fire. The third is the no-op test and the plan calls it the single most common defect in an always-on layer: a rule that restates what the model would do anyway costs context on every turn and delivers nothing.

Measured starting point 2026-07-26 at c175c1a: 7014/7209/7343 chars across AGENTS.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md, about 1070 words each.
acceptance_criteria: Given every line of the always-on baseline when it is audited then each line records whether a hook could enforce it and whether a glob could scope it and whether it changes behaviour versus the default and the no-op lines are named for removal

title: Declare scopes on the fragments the audit says earn them
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 4 step 2. Depends on the baseline audit and on the owner decision at plan §7.2.

Authoring work, not engine work. Verified 2026-07-26 at c175c1a: the path-scoped tier is fully built - schema.py:153 declares has_scope and exclude_scoped, planner.py:76 routes on them, claude.yaml declares a scoped_rules output at .claude/rules/{fragment_id}.md, and rule_md.j2 exists for both claude and codex. Zero of the 19 fragments declare a scope.

Candidates the plan names: subprocess discipline, test isolation, catalog authoring.

Blocking constraint. Scoping removes a fragment from the Claude and Copilot baselines but not from the Codex one, which inlines scoped fragments because our scopes are globs and nested AGENTS.md is directory-based. So each scoping is a deliberate removal from the github.com Copilot surface - a guarantee change per fragment, not a refactor - and plan §7.2 makes that an owner decision per fragment before anything moves.
acceptance_criteria: Given the fragments the audit named and the owner decision on the copilot surface when scopes are declared then each scoped fragment leaves the Claude and Copilot baselines and the Codex inlining is stated per fragment and the baseline size change is reported per agent family

title: Warn when a declared scope matches no file
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 4 step 3. The one missing check.

A scope whose globs match nothing is the only failure the existing gates cannot see: the fragment is well-formed, it projects, basicly check is green, and the rule never loads.

Warn at projection time, and error only where the technology is selected, so a docs-only consumer is not punished for having no Python.
acceptance_criteria: Given a fragment declaring a scope whose globs match no file when the catalog is projected then projection warns and given the same fragment in a repo where its technology is selected then the check errors with tests

title: Restructure the baseline for retrieval with a three-tier constraint block
description:
## Context

title: Stop one target's instruction file naming another target's enforcement mechanism
description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-30 by applying oh-my-openagent's forbidden-token gate idea to our own projected output
(`reference-repos/_analysis/oh-my-openagent.md`).

`.github/copilot-instructions.md:9` and `AGENTS.md:9` both carry:

> Force-push, history rewrite, destructive resets, `rm -rf`, and `.env*` reads/writes - hard-denied
> in `.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code; this rule covers other agents, so treat a blocked
> command as the answer.

`CLAUDE.md` does **not** carry it, so per-target variation already exists and is deliberate: the
Claude file omits the sentence because for Claude the deny-list is the actual mechanism rather than
something to describe.

The inverse is the defect. Copilot and any `AGENTS.md` reader are told about a file they will never
read and a mechanism that does not apply to them, then told the rule covers them anyway. The
author clearly considered it - the "this rule covers other agents" clause is there on purpose - so
this is imprecise wording rather than an oversight, and it is mild.

**Stated at its real size:** this is not a secrets leak and nothing sensitive is disclosed;
`.claude/settings.json` is a committed file. The cost is a sentence of always-on baseline spent
telling an agent about another agent's enforcement, in a baseline already measured at cap
(`always-on-baseline-at-cap`). The fix is to state the rule in terms of the reader - a blocked
command is the answer - and let the Claude target alone carry the mechanism.

Worth generalising while in there: whether any other fragment names one target's mechanism inside
another target's output. A cheap catalog-lint rule could check that a fragment body rendered into
target X does not reference target Y's config path, which is the transferable half of the
forbidden-token idea.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the projected instruction files when the confirmation-rules fragment is rendered then no target's output names another target's config path or enforcement mechanism, and the rule reads as a constraint on the agent reading it
acceptance_criteria: Given the projected instruction files when the confirmation-rules fragment is rendered then no target's output names another target's config path or enforcement mechanism and the rule reads as a constraint on the agent reading it

title: Record the external-review rules that three committed errors would have prevented
description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied
per the repo's retro rule. **Three distinct failures in one session share one root cause: reviewing an
external project without discipline.** All three reached committed files before being corrected.

1. **A README is a claim; the binary is the evidence.** I wrote into
   `docs/research/2026-07-26-sota-review.md` §2.11 that gastown ships a Bors-style merge queue that
   bisects to isolate a failing MR, and recommended building the same - from a fetched README summary.
   It is dead code: `AssembleBatch`/`ProcessBatch` have no call sites outside tests, the config field
   that enables them is never read, and the Go merge engine cannot be entered because its foreground
   mode hard-errors as deprecated while the real component is an agent working the queue sequentially.
   The corrected conclusion **inverted** the original.
2. **Read the licence before writing the adopt finding, not after.** In the same commit I wrote the
   warning that "deriving an implementation from a quoted snippet requires reading that project's
   LICENSE first" and then recommended porting ~400 lines from two repos whose licences had not been
   read. Both were restricted, and in **both cases the LICENSE file alone would have cleared them** -
   one hid a non-commercial Sustainable Use License with a per-subdirectory gap, the other put
   competition restrictions in `NOTICE.md`. That is three restricted repos in this reference set now.
3. **Correlation is not causation, and synthesis is where they get confused.** I wrote that every
   project adopting declarative phases traded away determinism, implying cause. Both failures were
   independent design errors in projects that also happened to be configurable. The decision to reject
   still held, on a different and better argument.

## The rules to record

- Before recommending adoption of a third-party feature, find its call sites; a symbol with no
  non-test caller does not ship, and neither does one behind a config flag nobody reads. Cite
  `file:line`, never a README line.
- Read every licence-bearing file including `NOTICE`, and check per-directory licences before assuming
  a monorepo is uniform - **before** writing adopt findings.
- A licence restricts copying expression, not learning a fact: measurements and concepts survive a
  restriction, implementations do not. That boundary is what keeps a competitive review usable.
- When a pattern appears across independent sources, state whether the mechanism is established or
  only the correlation.

## The open decision this bead must make, not assume

**Where these live is deliberately unsettled.** The obvious answer is a new on-demand skill
(`external-review` or similar), which costs nothing always-on - and the always-on baseline is at cap,
so that matters. But adding a 28th catalog skill is the wrong reflex right now: 27 existing skills have
never been invoked, and whether skills route at all is `basicly-m4zv.2`'s open question. Weigh at least
these before authoring anything:

- a new on-demand skill - zero always-on cost, but grows a catalog whose routing is unmeasured;
- a section in an existing skill - `catalog-authoring` is the closest fit and is already always-on for
  Copilot by a recorded decision;
- the **path-scoped rules tier**, which is built and almost unused, if a path predicate can express
  "editing a research or design document";
- prose in `docs/research/references.md` §2 only, accepting that a rule not in the catalog does not
  reach an agent that has not read that file.

Do not add always-on baseline text for this without measuring the delta - the tier exists precisely so
this class of conditional guidance costs nothing when it does not apply.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the four external-review rules when their home has been chosen and justified against the always-on baseline cost then they are authored in that home, projected, and an agent reviewing a third-party repository is told to verify call sites and read licences before writing an adopt finding
acceptance_criteria: Given the four external-review rules when their home has been chosen and justified against the always-on baseline cost then they are authored in that home projected and an agent reviewing a third-party repository is told to verify call sites and read licences before writing an adopt finding
close_reason: Four external-review rules authored as a new path-scoped design fragment scoped to docs/research/** and docs/design/**. Home justified by measured cost: Claude 7940 and Copilot 8074 unchanged (scoped fragments project to .claude/rules/ and are excluded from both baselines), so zero always-on cost on two of three surfaces; AGENTS.md pays +1618 because the codex target inlines scoped fragments for glob fidelity, leaving 10833 against its 12000 cap. Both globs match real files (2 + 7). Activation in the authoring session is not demonstrable because rules load at session start

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: [harness-decision] Home decided 2026-07-30 (session review, L3): the path-scoped rules tier, scoped to docs/research/** plus docs/design/** - the rules bind exactly when writing findings into those trees, cost zero always-on chars, and become the second real user of the built tier. Known cost accepted: codex inlines scoped fragments so AGENTS.md grows (8484 of 12000 today); measure and record the delta per this bead's AC. A new skill was rejected because 27 skills have never routed and routing is unmeasured until basicly-m4zv.2.

title: Warn that an unquoted list does not word-split in every shell
description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied.
An environment trap, so it earns exactly one bullet: the trap plus its avoidance.

**The incident.** Removing seventeen deferred blocking edges from the release epic, I wrote:

```sh
DEFER="basicly-jr0l.35 basicly-jr0l.40 ..."
for d in $DEFER; do uv run br dep remove basicly-m3od "$d"; done
```

In bash that iterates seventeen times. **This repo's shell is zsh, which does not word-split an
unquoted parameter expansion**, so the loop ran once with all seventeen ids as a single argument. The
command failed, and the failure was quiet in the way that matters: the loop printed one line, the
summary said `removed 0`, and only a separate re-count of the edges revealed nothing had happened. Had
I trusted the exit status or the absence of an error, the release scope would silently still be blocked
by seventeen beads.

**The avoidance**: write the list inline in the `for` header, or use an array (`arr=(a b c)` then
`for d in "${arr[@]}"`), or pipe through `xargs -n1`. Never iterate an unquoted scalar and assume
splitting.

**Why this is worth a catalog bullet rather than a note.** `non-interactive-shell.fragment.yaml`
already owns exactly this class - it exists because some shells alias `cp`/`mv`/`rm` to interactive
mode - and the fragment's own framing is "prefer cross-platform implementations over shell-specific
behavior when a choice exists". Word-splitting is the same shape: a construct that is correct in one
shell and silently wrong in another, on a repo that targets Windows, Linux and macOS and whose own
hooks run under whatever shell the host provides.

It also compounds with an existing recorded trap - `uv run` inside a shell for-loop returning empty
output, which already made a per-item audit report "all clean" falsely
(`batch-queries-over-cli-loops`). Both failures are the same lesson from different directions: a
shell loop over a list is where a silent no-op hides, so prefer one batch invocation and verify the
count changed.

**Cost check before authoring.** This fragment is always-on and the baseline is at cap, so keep it to
one bullet and measure the delta rather than adding a paragraph.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the non-interactive-shell guidance when it is read after this change then it warns that an unquoted parameter expansion does not word-split in every shell, names the array or inline-list avoidance, and the always-on baseline delta is measured and recorded
acceptance_criteria: Given the non-interactive-shell guidance when it is read after this change then it warns that an unquoted parameter expansion does not word-split in every shell names the array or inline-list avoidance and the always-on baseline delta is measured and recorded
close_reason: One bullet added to the non-interactive-shell fragment naming the zsh no-word-split trap plus the inline-list/array/batch avoidance and the verify-the-count check; verified in all three projected surfaces; baseline delta +282 chars each, leaving Claude 7940 and Copilot 8074 against the 9000 soft cap and AGENTS 9215 against 12000

title: loop: feature fan-in merge collides with child self-landing
description:
Found shipping basicly-ajq. loop._build_children fan-in merges every child worktree via merge.merge_queue once all children are closed — but a child driven through its own loop (the flow the harness-loop skill documents: advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes) leaves no worktree behind, so the parent's advance fails with "no worktree session named '<child>'" and the feature can never advance past build. Workaround used: record the parent verify gate directly (basicly verify --mode full --issue <id>), then approve ship and loop run.

Two coherent fixes; pick one and align the harness-loop skill with it:
(a) parent skips children whose branches are already merged (self-landing stays the documented child flow), or
(b) children stop self-landing (their loop ends at 'work committed'; the parent owns the merge queue) and the skill/docs change accordingly.

Chosen: (a) — in loop._build_children, filter merge-queue items to children with a live worktree session (worktree.list_sessions()); self-landed torn-down children count as already landed and are mentioned in the detail message.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a feature issue with two child tasks (br create --parent).
2. Drive each child through its own full loop: advance provisions its worktree, build/verify pass, advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes the child.
3. With all children closed and no child worktree sessions remaining, run `basicly loop advance <parent>` to trigger the build fan-in.
4. Observed: SystemExit "no worktree session named '<child>'" from merge.merge_queue; the feature can never advance past build. Expected: fan-in treats the self-landed children as already merged and advances build -> verify.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A feature whose children each landed and closed through their own loop advances build -> verify without manual gate recording
- merge_queue (or its caller) treats an already-merged, torn-down child as satisfied rather than an error
- A regression test covers the children-self-landed path
- The harness-loop skill's phase table matches the implemented flow

title: Resolve a declared tier into each projected agent surface that has a model slot
description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-31 after basicly-kjc5.58 landed. **Re-scoped the same day by the owner, who was right and
the first framing was wrong**: this is NOT claude-only. GitHub Copilot custom agents carry a per-agent
`model` field too, so at least claude AND copilot must be supported. Re-verified against live
authoritative docs rather than recall.

basicly-kjc5.59 is the resolution seam but its scope is `runner.py`/`run_record.py`/`config.py` - the
HEADLESS runner dispatch path, where a model is set by `_apply_model` via a `--model` flag or a
`{model}` placeholder. A natively spawned subagent never goes through that path: the host reads a
per-agent file and takes the model from frontmatter. basicly-kjc5.58 removed that line for every
family, so a declared tier is currently decorative for every natively spawned agent.

Concrete regression from kjc5.58, deliberate and known: the shipped `test-runner` declared
`model: haiku`, now declares `tier: low`, and `.claude/agents/test-runner.md` carries no model line, so
an agent whose own prose says "cheap and fast on purpose" inherits the session model on every spawn.
Verified: `rg '^model' .claude/agents/` matches nothing.

kjc5.58 was still right - the defect was a NON-PORTABLE value in a family-agnostic source. The fix is
to emit the resolved per-surface spelling, which is what basicly-kjc5.61's map must provide.

## Verified facts (live docs, 2026-07-31)

- **Claude Code** reads `.claude/agents/<slug>.md`; `model` takes a hyphenated id (`claude-haiku-4-5`)
  or a short alias (`haiku`), or `inherit`.
- **GitHub Copilot** custom agents live at `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root
  `agents/`). Frontmatter: `description` (required), `name`, `target` (`vscode`|`github-copilot`),
  `tools`, `model`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`; body
  capped at 30000 chars, which `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already matches.
- **Copilot's `model` value is a DISPLAY NAME**, not an id - `Claude Opus 4.5`, `Claude Sonnet 4` -
  and it accepts **a single string OR a prioritized array** tried in order
  (`model: ['Claude Opus 4.5', 'GPT-5.2']`). Our schema cannot express an ordered fallback list today.
- **VS Code reads BOTH** `.github/agents` and `.claude/agents` ("VS Code also detects `.md` files in the
  `.claude/agents` folder, following the Claude sub-agents format"). So basicly-ajq's rationale holds
  for VS Code but NOT for the Copilot cloud agent or Copilot CLI, which do not read `.claude/agents`.
- Copilot `tools` names differ from Claude's and are inconsistent across sources
  (`["read","search","edit"]` in the VS Code doc vs `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github` elsewhere), so
  a copilot projection needs a pinned tool-name mapping, not a copy.

## Prerequisite

The copilot half has no target file today: basicly still projects to `.claude/agents` only. Reopening
that is filed separately and must land first for the copilot half. The claude half is unblocked once
kjc5.61 lands.

## Open design decision for the owner

Per surface, either resolve the tier to that surface's own spelling and emit it, or emit nothing and
record that the tier was not honoured (the stance kjc5.59 already takes where a family has no slot).
Recommendation: resolve and emit wherever the surface has a model slot, because that is the only case
in which the tier vocabulary changes real behaviour instead of documenting an intention.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `.claude/agents/`, `tests/test_agents.py`.
acceptance_criteria: Given an agent source declaring a tier and a committed tier-to-model map when agents-build runs then every projected surface that has a per-agent model slot carries that surface's own spelling of the resolved model for that tier while a surface with no slot carries no model line and records that the tier was not honoured, and given a tier the map cannot resolve for a surface then the build refuses naming the source the surface and the tier rather than silently emitting no model, with tests

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: DYNAMIC INJECTION IS POSSIBLE ON CLAUDE CODE - PROVEN BY EXPERIMENT 2026-07-31. The owner asked whether the model could be left out of the projected file and injected before the host reads it, rather than baked in at build time. Answer: YES for claude code, via a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool. Three probes, each isolated with 'claude --settings <file>' so no live config was modified: (1) returning updatedInput {model: haiku} alone FAILED - the call lost its required fields; (2) returning updatedInput {description: ...} alone also FAILED with 'required parameter prompt is missing'. So on the Agent tool updatedInput REPLACES tool_input rather than merging, which CONTRADICTS the documented behaviour 'Object with fields to merge into tool_input ... Fields not present in updatedInput are left unchanged'. Worth knowing: that doc statement is false for this tool. (3) The working pattern - copy the whole tool_input dict, add model, return the lot - SUCCEEDED. Proof it took effect: the probe agent's frontmatter declared model: opus, the hook injected haiku, and the subagent's own transcript under projects/<proj>/<session>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl carries 22 messages all with model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, with ZERO occurrences of opus in any transcript of the run. The frontmatter was overridden. This is consistent with the documented resolution order, where the per-invocation model parameter (2) outranks the definition's frontmatter (3). Observed Agent tool_input keys: description, prompt, subagent_type, run_in_background - note model is ABSENT unless the caller sets it, which is why it must be added rather than rewritten. Robustness note: because the hook copies the input dict wholesale it forwards unknown and future fields verbatim, so a new required field upstream does not break it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD: there are now two viable mechanisms, not one. Static emission at agents-build time (this bead as originally scoped) OR a hook that resolves tier to model at spawn time from the committed map, leaving the projected file model-free. The hook variant is strictly more portable - a foreign harness needs only the map plus a ~15 line hook and no basicly code at all, which is the owner's stated plug-and-play goal - but it adds a process to the spawn path and is claude-code-specific as verified. The copilot equivalent is NOT yet verified: copilot custom agents and copilot CLI both document a hooks field (Preview) and that needs its own probe before any claim. Do not assume symmetry.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: COPILOT CLI HOOK INJECTION DOES NOT WORK TODAY - tested 2026-07-31 at the owner's request. Copilot DOES document the capability: the hooks reference gives preToolUse an output schema of permissionDecision (allow|deny|ask), permissionDecisionReason, and modifiedArgs described as 'tool arguments to use instead of the originals' - i.e. argument substitution is specified. Documented CLI config locations: repo-level .github/hooks/NAME.json, user-level ~/.copilot/hooks/ (or COPILOT_HOME), plus policy.d and inline settings. BUT on the installed CLI the hook never fires. Three probes from a scratch repo containing .github/hooks/tierprobe.json with a preToolUse command hook that logged every payload and returned allow: (1) delegating to a custom agent - hook did not fire; (2) a plain shell tool with --allow-all-tools - did not fire; (3) the same shell tool WITHOUT --allow-all-tools, to rule out the permission pipeline being bypassed - did not fire. Zero payloads captured in any run, so this is not about which tool is intercepted; the repo-level hook config is simply not being loaded or run. Note 'hook' does not appear anywhere in copilot --help, and experimental was already true in settings. LIKELY EXPLANATION, not yet confirmed: the modifiedArgs capability is documented under the copilot-SDK hooks path (/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/hooks/pre-tool-use), so it may be an SDK-only feature rather than a CLI one. Do not assume the CLI will grow it. VERSION DRIFT WORTH KNOWING: the binary reported 1.0.75 earlier in the same session and 1.0.77 by the end - it self-updates, so a pinned version in prose rots by itself and per-run adapter_version capture (which the runner already does) is the right design. WHAT DOES WORK ON COPILOT: static frontmatter. Verified twice - the /agent listing validated a declared model value, and a custom agent declaring NO model printed 'Tierprobe(claude-opus-5)' in the CLI transcript, i.e. it inherited the session model. Also note copilot prints the resolved model in its delegation line, which is a free observation channel for verifying any future mechanism. CONSEQUENCE: for a first version the mechanism is necessarily HYBRID - claude gets dynamic hook injection (proven working), copilot gets static frontmatter emission (proven working) plus session-level control via copilot --model for harness-launched sessions. That is not the uniform design the owner would prefer but it is what the two hosts actually support today.

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: CORRECTION - COPILOT HOOK INJECTION DOES WORK. The earlier comment on this bead concluded copilot CLI hooks never fire. That was WRONG, and the cause was the config LOCATION, not the capability. Repo-level .github/hooks/hooks.json is NOT loaded by copilot CLI 1.0.77 (retested with the canonical filename, with inline bash instead of a script path, and inside a real git repo - sessionStart did not fire either, so it was not about tool matching). User-level ~/.copilot/hooks/hooks.json IS loaded and fires. Also retracted: I claimed the CLI binary contains no hook identifiers based on a strings scan. That evidence was worthless - a control check showed strings I had directly observed the CLI emitting (allow-all-tools, premiumRequests, modelMetrics) also return zero matches, because the JS payload is a compressed bundle. The conclusion rests on behaviour only. PROVEN END TO END on copilot: the agent-spawn tool is named 'task' with args agent_type, description, mode, name, prompt - and NO model key, so model must be ADDED not rewritten, same as claude. A preToolUse hook matching toolName 'task' that returns modifiedArgs containing all original args PLUS model ran a custom agent declaring NO model on the injected model: the CLI delegation line printed Tierprobe(claude-haiku-4.5) where the session model was claude-opus-5. Copilot prints the resolved model in that line, which is a free verification channel. PER-HOST DIFFERENCES to encode: hook event PreToolUse vs preToolUse; tool name Agent vs task; rewrite field updatedInput vs modifiedArgs; payload tool_input as an OBJECT vs toolArgs as a JSON STRING that must be parsed first; model spelling claude-haiku-4-5 or the alias haiku vs the dotted claude-haiku-4.5; observation channel the subagent transcript vs the printed delegation line. Both REPLACE rather than merge, so both hooks must echo the full argument set back. IMPORTANT DESIGN CONSTRAINT for basicly-wbsz: because copilot only honours the hook at USER level, it applies to every repo on the machine. So the hook cannot assume a map is present - it must resolve against the current working directory and NO-OP silently, leaving the call untouched, whenever the cwd has no committed map. It also cannot be delivered by repo projection the way our other artifacts are; it needs a per-machine install step.

title: Add 'enforced_by' schema field + enforcement-pointer lint (§3.1)
description: §3.1/§11.4: context minimalism has no mechanical check. Add an 'enforced_by' field to the fragment schema and a lint that flags prose restating a mechanically-enforced rule instead of pointing at the command/config.
close_reason: Added enforced_by list to fragment schema + Fragment dataclass, parse/type-validate in loader, and a 4th catalog-lint rule requiring each enforced_by command to be cited in the body (§3.1). 8 tests added; full gate green (ruff/pyright/pytest 257, catalog-lint/check/skills-check); dogfooded violate=exit1 / cite=exit0. Committed 233419e. Unblocks basicly-ihs.

title: commit-messages CI gate checks only the subject and misses body-trailer bead ids
description:
## Problem

The quality-gates commit-messages job feeds only the commit SUBJECT (git log %s) to beads-commit-msg.py, but the repo convention puts the beads issue id as a trailing BODY line (and dotted child ids like basicly-onb.6.2 cannot appear in the subject per the conventional-commits rules). So every commit with the id in the body fails CI with 'Missing/unknown beads issue id', even though the local commit-msg hooks (which see the full message) pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

- CI validates the full commit message (subject + body), matching the local commit-msg hooks
- A commit with the beads id in a trailing body line passes the CI commit-messages gate
- The previously-failing commit 5b5f3e9 passes under the fixed check
close_reason: Fixed the commit-messages CI gate to validate the full commit message (git log %B) instead of only the subject (%s), matching the local commit-msg hooks. Verified by simulating the fixed loop over the last 6 commits (all pass, including the previously-failing 5b5f3e9).

title: Catalog selection / flavors (install fragments+hooks but not skills)
description:
§9/§11.8: let a consumer choose a subset of the catalog at install time. Design settled 2026-07-16 (see comment): technology scoping — sources carry an optional `technologies:` list (absent = universal, always ships); install records the repo's selection in `basicly.toml` (default: all); projection commands filter unselected sources and the manifest sweep removes outputs a narrowed selection excludes; core sync stays full. Tag vocabulary is a controlled list enforced by catalog-lint. v2 (out of scope): per-block technology conditioning inside agent slots.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Catalog sources (skills, fragments, agents-fragments, hooks) accept an optional `technologies:` list; a source without it is universal and always projected
- catalog-lint rejects a `technologies:` value outside the controlled vocabulary (stack tags like python/go plus environment tools like zsh/tmux/starship/wezterm)
- `basicly install` accepts a technology-selection flag and records the selection in `basicly.toml`; omitting it selects everything (current behavior unchanged)
- `basicly build` / `skills-build` / `agents-build` / `hooks-build` skip sources whose `technologies:` has no overlap with the recorded selection; core sync still copies the full catalog
- Narrowing the selection then rebuilding sweeps the now-excluded projections via the manifest (no stale outputs left)
- A repo with no selection recorded in `basicly.toml` projects the full catalog (backward compatible)
- Regression tests cover: universal source always ships, tagged source filtered out, selection recorded/read from basicly.toml, sweep after narrowing, lint rejection of unknown tags
- docs/architecture.md documents the property, the selection, and the filtering point

comments.author: niksa
comments.text: Design settled with the user (2026-07-16), superseding the kind-level framing: technology scoping. Sources (skills, fragments, agents, hooks) get an optional 'technologies: [go, java, python, ...]' property; absent means universal and always ships. Install flag records the repo's selection in basicly.toml (default: all); build/skills-build/agents-build/hooks-build filter unselected sources at projection time (core sync stays full for provenance-simple upgrades), and the manifest sweeps projections a narrowed selection excludes. Tag vocabulary is a controlled list enforced by catalog-lint; environment tools (zsh, tmux, starship, wezterm) use the same mechanism as stack tags. v2 (explicitly out of v1 scope): per-block technology conditioning inside agent slots. Agreed motivation: a non-Python consumer should not receive tool-uv et al.; see the verification discussion on 2026-07-16 (core fragments/agents are already stack-clean, the skills pack is the residual). Priority recommendation recorded: 2f4 -> a3d -> aff -> v0.1.3 + consumer refresh -> 7ca.

title: Phase 1 buy the numbers that decide the expensive phases
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 1. Depends on Phase 0 for 1b and 1c. Size 3-4 sessions.

Three assumptions carry large downstream work and each has a cheap test; at least one could cancel a whole phase. 1a (recall) is independent and can run first. 1b (7bur, cost per landed package) is the hub - the design documents defer four further decisions to it, and kjc5.29 must land first so tier economics are not measured against an unpinned model mapping. 1c (localisation) must precede Phase 5 because it changes what the decomposer scope declarations have to carry.

Risk: 1b is a genuine build, not a measurement script, and is the item most likely to slip. Hard constraint carried over - the eval must not cost more than the thing it measures.
acceptance_criteria: Given the three Phase 1 measurements are run when the phase closes then each number is written into the design document that owns it and the roster tier table and the localisation question are decided by data rather than argument

title: Measure always-on recall per agent family against a no-guidance control
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 1 item 1a. Independent - can run first or in parallel with anything.

Open a fresh session per agent family and ask the agent to summarise the rules in the always-on file; anything it cannot recall is not doing work. Formalise it as a behavioural recall case whose no-guidance control arm is the same session with the baseline absent.

This decides whether Phase 4 is urgent surgery or routine tidying, and per architecture §14.4 no change to the always-on cap in either direction is legitimate until it runs.

Measured starting point 2026-07-26 at c175c1a: AGENTS.md 7014 chars, .claude/CLAUDE.md 7209, .github/copilot-instructions.md 7343 - about 1070 words each against the 9000 max_size_warning. The cliff concern stands (1070 words is well past the ~500-word threshold the review cites); the plan §2 headroom figure does not.
acceptance_criteria: Given a fresh session per agent family when the agent is asked to summarise the rules in its always-on file then recall is scored per rule against a no-guidance control arm that is the same session with the baseline absent and the result is written into steering-surfaces-design.md section 2.2

title: Measure whether AST-derived localisation cuts an implementers pre-first-edit tokens
description:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 1 item 1c. New work, no prior bead. Depends on 7bur. Must run before Phase 5.

Does an AST-derived localisation artifact - tree-sitter, no model, no tokens - measurably reduce an implementer pre-first-edit token share?

It changes what the decomposer scope declarations have to carry: if the engine can derive reachable surface, the decomposer declares intent and boundaries instead of enumerating files. That is Dana contract in the roster design (agent-roster-design.md:270), which is why this gates Phase 5.

Note the framing. The cheap-tier pre-reader persona was rejected (architecture §14.7) for being a model whose omissions are undetectable; a parser coverage is a checkable property, which is the whole difference.
acceptance_criteria: Given a set of implementer dispatches when each is run with and without an AST-derived localisation artifact then the pre-first-edit token share is reported for both arms and the parser coverage is stated as a checkable property and the result decides whether the decomposer declares intent and boundaries or enumerates files

title: agents as a catalog kind: compose subagent files from building-block fragments
description:
Gap (user, 2026-07-16): basicly projects fragments, skills, and hooks — but not agent files. Subagent definitions (.claude/agents/*.md) are hand-authored per repo with no single source of truth, so they drift and cannot be centrally improved.

Vision: agent files become generated artifacts composed by the projector from an essential-blocks taxonomy (candidate blocks: security, planning, git, orchestration, conventions, documentation, hygiene, hardening, enforcement, verify, validate, authorize, authenticate, context, work tracking, work scoping, review, gates). Core blocks are owned by basicly devs; consumers extend or override specific blocks with custom building blocks via the .basicly-local overlay — the same core/overlay model fragments already use. Generated agent files carry the generated marker, are gated by protect-generated, and must never be edited manually.

Emission is single-source per the 2f4 policy: .claude/agents/ only — VS Code parses the Claude sub-agent format natively (user-shared research finding, 2026-07-16), and Claude Code reads only .claude/.

Prerequisite research: the 84v SOTA research covered instruction-file blocks, not subagent-file anatomy. A dedicated research pass (Anthropic sub-agents spec + VS Code custom-agent docs + curated corpus: awesome-claude-code, VoltAgent/awesome-claude-code-subagents, wshobson/agents) must establish the frontmatter contract, the recurring body anatomy, and a frequency-ranked block taxonomy before the schema is designed. Findings land as comments on this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Research findings recorded on this bead: frontmatter contract, cross-tool field compatibility, body anatomy, ranked building-block taxonomy mapped to the candidate list
- New agents catalog kind: YAML sources in .basicly/core (schema + catalog-lint coverage + scaffold command consistent with skills-new/fragment-new)
- Projector composes and renders .claude/agents/*.md with the generated marker; protect-generated blocks manual edits
- Overlay can add whole agents and extend/override individual blocks of core agents
- basicly check/build/install/uninstall handle the new kind (manifest-tracked, stale-file sweep)
- docs/architecture.md documents the kind, the composition model, and the single-source emission policy
- Tests cover schema validation, composition/override precedence, rendering, and the sweep
